en: The Legend of Suvarṇavarṇa. Volume One. Om, homage to the Buddha!
Sva Roy 1,1–5 [1] Thus it is heard: after the Elder Mahākāśyapa had passed into parinirvāṇa, the great-souled Elder Ānanda, who was endowed with wisdom equal to that of Śāradvatīputra,
out of compassion— just like the Tathāgata— [visited] those various villages, cities, market towns, hamlets, ports, and so forth, and [taught] them...
He disciplined those to be trained by means of various specific methods.

Then, at another time, out of regard for those to be trained, while satisfying many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings with the sprinkling of the nectar-rain of the teaching of the True Dharma, he was dwelling in Vaiśālī in the Āmrapālī grove.

Now at that time, there lived in the city of Rājagṛha a caravan leader named Divākara, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her;
yet, as he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself, neither a son nor a daughter was born to him.
Being childless, he was anxious and tormented by the desire for a son.

Then, five omens appeared to a certain son of the gods among the Thirty-three, one who was distinguished by his great merit and power. Having beheld the world adorned by the arising of a Buddha, that god, longing for nirvāṇa, desired to take rebirth among human beings.

Śakra, the lord of the gods, saw that son of the gods subject to the law of decline; having observed that the world was adorned by the appearance of a Buddha, he, desiring nirvāṇa, wished to take rebirth among human beings. Having seen this, [he spoke].
And furthermore, having approached that son of the gods,
he said: "Friend, if you desire to take rebirth among humans,
take rebirth in the city of Rājagṛha, in the womb of the wife of the caravan leader Divākara."
He said, "Kauśika, that caravan leader is faithless; he has no serene confidence in the Buddha.
Śakra replied, "Friend, take it! I shall act in such a way that this caravan leader will develop serene confidence in the teaching of the Buddha."
The son of the gods said:
"Kauśika, if that caravan leader, together with his wife, were to go for refuge to the Three Jewels for as long as he lives, then I would take rebirth in the womb of that caravan leader’s wife."
[4] Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, descended from among the Trāyastriṃśa gods into the sky above the city of Rājagṛha, and alighted upon the upper terrace of the merchant Divākara’s house.

By the power of the majesty of Śakra, the lord of the gods, the entire house was seen to be illuminated by a divine radiance. Upon seeing this divine light, the merchant Divākara, his eyes wide with wonder, looked toward the four quarters.

He began to look around, and as soon as he saw Śakra, the lord of the gods, he immediately prostrated at his feet and said: "O Lord of Gods, I have gained a great gain; I have been truly blessed that you have come to my home, for this house has been purified by your arrival."
"Therefore, let it be commanded: what is the purpose of your coming? Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, replied:
"O caravan leader, you are childless and long for a son; therefore, from this day forward, together with your wife, take refuge in the Three Jewels for as long as you live."
"A son shall be born to you."
Divākara the caravan leader, joyful, satisfied, and elated in mind, said:

"O Lord of Gods, I shall do exactly as you command; from this day forward, for as long as I live, I, together with my wife, go for refuge to the Three Jewels. Then Śakra, the Lord of Gods, [addressed] Divākara the caravan leader and his wife.

Having established him in the taking of refuge, he vanished from Rājagṛha and reappeared among the Trāyastriṃśa gods. In the palace of that son of the gods, Śakra, the lord of the gods, related this matter to him in detail.
[5] Eventually, that son of the gods, having passed away from among the Trāyastriṃśa deities, descended into the womb of the wife of the caravan leader Divākara in the city of Rājagṛha.
From the very moment he entered her womb, a supreme abundance of beauty appeared in the body of that caravan leader’s wife,
and a delightful fragrance began to waft forth.
There are five unique qualities found in certain women of wise nature.
What are the five?
She knows when a man is impassioned.
He knows when one is dispassionate;
he knows the time;
he knows the season.
He knows when the embryo has entered the womb;
he knows from whom the embryo has descended;
and he knows whether it is a male child.
He knows whether it is a girl;
if it is a boy, he remains resting against the right side of the womb;
if it is a girl, [she rests against the left].
Having emerged from her left side, it remained there;
she, being exceedingly joyful, announced it to her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, you prosper!"

"I have become pregnant; and since it remains resting against my right side, it will certainly be a boy. Having heard this, he too was filled with joy; straightening his upper body and extending his right arm, he uttered this exclamation:

"May I indeed behold the face of a son long desired; may one be born to me who is not base-born; may he perform my duties, support me when I am supported, and receive my inheritance. May my family lineage endure for a long time. And after we have passed away, may someone give gifts, whether small or great, perform meritorious deeds, and dedicate the merit in our names, saying:
'May this follow those two wherever they go, according to their rebirth.'"
Knowing that she had conceived, he kept her in the upper story of the palace,
unconfined; he provided her with cold refreshments in the cold season and warm refreshments in the hot season, and with food prescribed by physicians that was neither too bitter nor too sour.
With food that was not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent, and not too astringent— being free from the tastes of bitter, sour, salty, sweet, pungent, and astringent—
he saw her whose limbs were adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, never descending from couch to couch or seat to seat to the ground below.
And for her, there was no hearing of any unpleasant sound whatsoever until the fetus reached full maturity.
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.

Endowed with an abundance of complexion, the color of refined gold, he captivated the minds and eyes of all people; his body was draped in golden-yellow garments, and from his entire body the fragrance of sandalwood wafted forth,
while from his mouth the scent of a blue lotus issued.
As soon as he was born, a rain of garments and a rain of *karṇikāra* flowers fell upon that house;
and those garments were the color of gold.
[7] Then, having seen that most wonderful thing and the perfection of his noble physical form, Divākara the caravan leader, along with his wife and retinue, were struck with supreme amazement.
Divākara the caravan leader was standing outside the house in the gateway courtyard when it was announced to him: "Caravan leader, congratulations; a son has been born!"
Joyful, satisfied, and with an exalted mind, he entered his home and beheld the prince, who was exceedingly handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; endowed with all major and minor limbs,

possessed of a wealth of complexion like the color of refined gold, captivating the minds and eyes of all people, his body veiled in yellow-gold garments, and from his body issued the fragrance of sandalwood.
And from his mouth there wafted the fragrance of a blue lotus;
a rain of garments and a rain of *karṇikāra* flowers fell.
Seeing those garments, which were the color of gold, he again, with supreme joy and gladness, uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).
"Oh, what a gain I have obtained! Oh, how my heart's desire has been fulfilled, since such a son, renowned for his great merit, has been born to me!
With a mind thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, he gave those garments to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, friends, relatives, and kinsmen.
[8] For that prince, after having performed an extensive birth festival for twenty-one days—three times seven days—once he was born, the establishment of his name was undertaken.
"What shall be the name of this boy? the kinsmen asked. They said, "This prince is endowed with an abundance of complexion, like the color of refined gold."

Therefore, let the prince’s name be Suvarṇavarṇa; thus the name Suvarṇavarṇa was established. Prince Suvarṇavarṇa was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to clean him, and two to play with him. He grew rapidly, like a lotus in a pond, until he reached adulthood. When he was grown...
Having grown up, he was then introduced to writing, as well as to arithmetic, calculation, finger-reckoning, subtraction, depositing, and entrusting; and in the examination of goods,

the examination of cloth, the examination of elephants, the examination of horses, the examination of wood, the examination of gems, the examination of young men, and the examination of young women— he became an expert in these eight examinations, both in opening [the seals] and in reading [the texts].
He became a wise man of sharp conduct;
he was faithful, noble, and of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others.
Compassionate, magnanimous, desirous of the Dharma, and affectionate toward sentient beings, he had studied the treatises.
Being one of such supreme merit and great power,
whatever he thinks of or whatever wealth, such as clothing and so forth, he prays for— all that is accomplished exactly so.
However, he did not recognize that "I alone am one of great merit and power.

And the caravan leader Divākara, through the power of taking refuge in the Three Jewels, thought, "My son has been born," and with even greater measure he became devoted to the teaching of the Blessed One; from time to time, he performed acts of service for the teaching of the Blessed One.
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, a caravan leader named Vimala arrived from the great ocean with his ship successfully completed its voyage.
Having fed the Buddha, the Blessed One, along with a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty monks, he provided each individual monk with...

Clothed in his three robes, the entire world was filled with his fame; the caravan’s journey across the great ocean became fruitful, and the title of "caravan leader" was realized by him who had thus performed services for the teaching of the Blessed One.
Upon hearing this, rivalry arose in Divākara the caravan leader.
I too shall embark upon the great ocean;
and if I return from there with my ship successfully completed,
I shall inform all the disciples of the Blessed One who dwell in Jambūdvīpa, having requested them on behalf of the Blessed One.
"Having gathered them all together at once and satisfied them with excellent food, I shall clothe each individual monk with a set of three robes of great value.
He reported this matter to his wife,
and she said, "My lord, may your intentions be fulfilled!"
"May my heart's desires be fulfilled!

Then the caravan leader Divākara, having caused a proclamation by bell to be made three times in the city of Rājagṛha, set out upon the great ocean accompanied by five hundred merchants; and while he had thus embarked upon that great ocean—
The Blessed One had entered parinirvāṇa; while he was still staying there, the Elder Mahākāśyapa also entered parinirvāṇa.
Then, at another time, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa went to the Bamboo Grove, where a monk was reciting verses connected with impermanence.
Life, whether one is moving or standing, by day or by night, flows away like the current of great rivers; it goes on and never returns.
For those who dwell through the nights, life becomes ever more diminished.
And for fish in shallow water, what pleasure could there possibly be?
(2) This form is utterly decayed, a nest of diseases, and fragile; it will break apart as a mass of putridity, for life indeed ends in death. (3)
Alas, before long this body shall lie upon the earth—empty, devoid of consciousness, like discarded straw. What is the use of this body that is constantly discharging putridity? 4.
"Constantly overcome by disease, fearing old age and death,
with this putrid body that is fragile and afflicted—
one seeks the supreme peace, the unsurpassed security and well-being. (5–6)
Sva Roy 21,3–23,1 [11] Then, having heard these verses, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa became agitated; seeing the advantages of nirvāṇa over cyclic existence (saṃsāra),
he paid homage to that monk and asked him:

"Noble one, what is this? the monk was asked. "Venerable sir, it is the word of the Buddha," he replied. Upon hearing this, a great faith arose in him toward the teaching of the Blessed One, as well as a longing for the going-forth and a longing for liberation.
Then, having paid honor to that monk and fallen at his feet, he said: "Noble one, I wish to go forth."
"Out of compassion for him, you ought to grant me ordination.
The monk asked, "Venerable one, have you been permitted by your mother and father?
He replied, "No."
The monk said, "Go, venerable one, and first look after your parents; for we do not ordain anyone who has not been permitted by his parents.
He replied, "I shall do so."

[12] Then the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, his mind distressed by the fear of cyclic existence, went to his own residence, prostrated at his mother’s feet, and said: "Mother, give me your permission; I shall go forth into homelessness in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Upon hearing this, his mother fell into a state of extreme despondency.
Striking him on the chest, she said:
"Son, you are my only son—dear, beloved, handsome, and never disagreeable; you were obtained through hundreds of aspirations. How can you renounce the world and leave me behind?"
He said, "Mother, separation from what is dear is inevitable; therefore, give me your permission, for I shall go forth into homelessness in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Upon hearing this, a great sense of spiritual urgency arose within her, and with a throat choked with tears, she said, "Son, do not say this to me even a third time!"
"Lest hot blood should issue from my mouth," she reflected;
"given the nature of his resolve, I will not be able to turn him back."
"I shall devise a stratagem.
Then she said,
"Son, your father, thinking he would perform meritorious service for the Buddha's teaching, has set out upon the great ocean."
"As long as he does not arrive, I will not grant you permission;
if he has arrived, he will grant you permission, and then you may go forth."
Devoted to his mother, he reflected:
"If I speak to her again, she might perhaps experience great distress;
therefore, I shall remain here until my father returns."
He remained silent.
And whenever the youth Suvarṇavarṇa descended onto the street,
the people, beholding the perfection of his noble form, could not reach satiety while gazing upon him.

He became beloved by the great multitude of people; seeing that his mind was completely turned away from sensual desires, drawn by the excellence of his noble form, his mother reflected: "Alas, what a tragedy! With such a resolve as this, he will surely abandon me and go forth into homelessness even now.
Thereupon, with a mind constantly filled with apprehension, she began to act in accordance with his inclinations.
The youth Suvarṇavarṇa constantly attended upon wise ascetics and brahmins;
there he heard whatever was well-spoken that was conducive to the measure of liberation.
He writes in that book:
"Outside the city of Rājagṛha, there is a park belonging to the merchant-diviner Divākara, endowed with flowers, fruits, and water.
There, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa goes day after day to that paternal park and remains reading the book of well-spoken verses."

Now at that time, there lived in the city of Rājagṛha a courtesan named Kāśisundarī, who was endowed with feminine beauty and youth and was beloved by the great multitude. There was also a minister of King Ajātaśatru named Pracaṇḍa, who was highly esteemed by that king.
His mind was exceedingly infatuated with the maiden Kāśisundarī; day after day he went to his own pleasure garden with her and enjoyed amorous play.
Sva Roy 28,1–31,4 [14]: Then, at another time, the maiden Kāśisundarī, adorned with all her ornaments, departed from Rājagṛha and set out for the park of the minister Pracaṇḍa.
And the prince Suvarṇavarṇa, having departed from the city of Rājagṛha, was going to his own park.

The maiden Kāśisundarī saw the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, who was exceedingly handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; he was endowed with all major and minor limbs and possessed a profusion of complexion like the color of refined gold.
Seeing him, who captivated the minds and eyes of all people, his body draped in yellow garments of golden hue, this thought occurred to her:
"Oh, what a perfection of noble form!
Oh, what a profusion of beauty! Blessed indeed is that woman who shall have him as her husband.
Thus she thought, being utterly captivated by him.
"Unfortunate is that woman who does not experience the pleasures of love with such a man as this! We are women who live by our beauty;
this prince is endowed with the freshness of youth and is common to all men."
"What if I were to entice him in such a way that there might be a union between me and him? Having thought this, she stood before him and began to display seductive gestures.
However, because that Great Being was by his very nature averse to sensual desire and inclined toward Nirvana, he paid her no heed.
Sva Roy 31,4–35 [15]: She reflected, "Surely he is ashamed;
for that reason he does not pay attention to me here. Since he has set out for the park, I too shall go right there."
Thinking, "I shall entice him there in secret," she followed behind him; she was noticed by the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, who entered ahead of her and closed the gate of that garden.
The maiden Kāśisundarī said:
"O Prince, how can this be right?
I have come for your sake;
it is not fitting for you to display such harshness toward me."
He did not give her any reply at all.
She reflected:
"In this matter, there must be two possibilities."
Or perhaps he is utterly indifferent to desires;
or perhaps he is overcome by great dejection.
In any case, it is not possible for me to win him over through beauty or speech; I shall win him over through touch.
And seeing me, he closes the gate.
What means might there be by which I could approach him in secret?
Or rather, without his knowledge, I shall come tomorrow morning first, enter this garden, and remain there.
"I shall so gratify him when he comes to me with embraces and other such physical contacts that he will come under my control.
Having reflected thus, she returned and entered the city;
on that day, she did not go to the garden of the minister Pracaṇḍa.

[16] Although the minister Pracaṇḍa was waiting for her in his own garden, he became weary after a long time; at the hour of the sun’s setting, he entered the city and dispatched a messenger to his own house regarding Kāśisundarī, asking: "For what reason have you not come today?"

"The maiden Kāśisundarī made an excuse, saying, 'Noble son, today a headache afflicts me so severely that I did not come to the garden. Then another person informed the world— consisting of friends, enemies, and neutrals— "
"It is not that her headache afflicts her; rather, she went to the park to visit the youth Suvarṇavarṇa.
As she was returning from that park, I saw her.
Upon hearing this, a state of intense anger arose within the minister Pracaṇḍa.
Then he reflected: "I shall bring about such a disaster that tomorrow the maiden Kāśisundarī and the prince Suvarṇavarṇa will no longer exist."
"Among all enmities, this is indeed the most base: namely, enmity toward women.
With his heart burning with the fire of anger, he passed those nights in great distress.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, he addressed a certain trusted man:

"Take my sword; I shall go to the park outside Rājagṛha, for I have a certain urgent business there. "Very well, Master," replied the man, and taking the sword, he followed behind him. Then the minister Pracaṇḍa, having departed from Rājagṛha with that man, entered the park belonging to the caravan leader Divākara and stayed there.
[17] The maiden Kāśisundarī also, her body adorned with various garments and ornaments, departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to the park of the caravan leader Divākara.
Having entered there, she saw the minister Pracaṇḍa; upon seeing him, she became terrified.
She reflected, "This man is fierce by nature; he will surely cause me great misfortune today," and she desired to turn back.

Then the minister Pracaṇḍa, seeing her, his mind ablaze with the fire of anger, knitted his brows into a three-pronged frown upon his forehead and rushed forward. Thereupon, seizing her by the hair with impetuosity, he cast her down face-down upon the ground without mercy.
Having thrown him down, he dragged him toward himself and spoke thus: "Having come here, you consort with the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, yet you say this to me:
'A headache afflicts me exceedingly.'"
"Since she has not come into your presence,
today I shall impose such a bond of restriction upon you that you shall never again behold the world of the living;
I shall cause you to sport with the youth Suvarṇavarṇa."

Hearing this, the maiden Kāśisundarī, disregarding the pain born of being dragged back and forth and terrified by the fear of death, her throat choked with sobs, cried out, "Alas! and, with trembling limbs, fell at the feet of the minister Pracaṇḍa. With words that were piteous, wretched, and faltering, she said, "May the noble son be gracious; you ought not to have me executed, for women are always offenders."
"From this moment forth, I shall never do such a thing again;
for as long as I live, I shall be your slave.
Therefore, enough of this rashness; grant me my life."
As that evil-minded man spoke thus in words that were piteous, wretched, and faltering, the fire of his anger increased all the more.
Then he said to his companion: "Quickly, with this sword, cut off her head at the roots and cast it upon the ground!"
Sva Roy 39,1–43,2 [18] Then that man, having heard the wicked words and ill-spoken speech of that evil-minded one, began to tremble and thought:
"Alas, what cruelty! For this woman has served him in many ways; how then can he wish to have her executed for the sake of such a trivial offense?
Alas, even we are terrified by the fear for our livelihood, since we remain at the side of this lowest of men, who is like a venomous serpent!"

"In every way, I have fallen into a great peril. What is the proper course here? Or rather, I shall speak to him plainly; perhaps, being addressed plainly, he might turn back from this evil and false path.

Having realized this, his mind filled with agitation, his heart melted by those most piteous lamentations of the woman, his eyes overflowing with tears, and joining his palms in supplication, he [addressed] the minister Pracaṇḍa.
He said:
"May my lord be gracious; you ought not to employ me in such an unworthy task. I am neither a Niṣāda nor an executioner.
For how indeed can my lord deceive me into performing that deed which even the minds of executioners do not venture to undertake?"

Moreover, this woman is exceedingly famous, beautiful to behold, lovely, and skilled in all the arts; she is extremely beloved by the refined people residing in Rājagṛha as well as those who have arrived from various regions and countries.

This is a common object of pleasure for human beings. How indeed, my lord, can aversion arise in a wise and discerning man toward such an object of affection? Therefore, enough with this resolve, which brings about opposition in both worlds!
Be gracious; you ought not to consume both me and yourself with this fire of misconduct. Moreover, my lord, she is of delicate limbs and endowed with beauty and youth.
I consider this joy of men to be as if it were embodied.
O Lord, this [joy], through its most piteous, wretched, and sweet words, makes a request to you; it pierces my heart. (1–2)
My heart trembles today upon hearing your fiery words;
who could he be with such a pitiless mind that he strives to kill her? Even the most merciless Mlecchas would not venture to kill her.
O Lord, how could my mind ever venture to kill her, toward whom even the beasts feel great compassion upon seeing her? What man, being human himself, would strike her with a weapon? (4-5)
"Therefore, be gracious; it is improper for you even to hear these words, let alone to perform this most cruel deed, O Lord.
[19] Then that evil-minded man, because his intentions were already perverted, did not regain his composure even when addressed by that man with such heart-warming words.
And with a face made fierce by the knitting of his brows in a frown of anger, he spoke to that man.
"O man, what favor do you have toward her that, having transgressed my command, you do not wish to have her executed?
If you will indeed have her executed, it will be well for us; but if you will not have her executed, your life shall end this very day."
Then that man, perceiving his harsh resolve, became afraid and began to reflect:
"Alas, I have entered into a most perilous situation!
If I do not carry out his command, he will certainly deprive me of my life this very day."
"How could he not kill me, when he is prepared to kill such a woman—a woman who has been enjoyed in so many ways?
How can this be? How indeed can I consider myself a man, yet bring a weapon down upon the body of such a woman, the most beautiful in the land?"

Having made the firm resolve, "In every way, my own life may perish, but I shall never strike her," the thought occurred to him: "If I were to take up my sword and flee, in this way I would have protected myself and the maiden Kāśisundarī."
Taking his sword, he departed from that garden and fled with all his speed;
the minister Pracaṇḍa also followed close behind him as far as the gateway.
[20] Then the maiden Kāśisundarī, considering herself as if her life had returned after having departed, rose up very quickly and approached the vicinity of the wall, thinking, "I shall flee.
However, she was unable to leap over the high wall.
And the minister Pracaṇḍa, having turned back, did not see the maiden Kāśisundarī in that place.
He began to look here and there until he saw her approaching near the wall; he then started to go toward her with great haste.
There, however, a black snake was stationed;
it bit her on the right foot, and seeing this, he fled.
The maiden Kāśisundarī reflected:
"This Pracaṇḍa will come and kill me. With her mind fixed on that thought and terrified by the fear of death, she did not perceive anything else.
"I have been bitten by a black cobra! Thus she cried.
And the minister Pracaṇḍa arrived at that thicket of *atimuktaka* creepers;

then that evil-souled one, whose heart was pitiless and whose mind was agitated by intense hatred, dragged the maiden Kāśisundarī out from that thicket of *atimuktaka* creepers and [struck] her on the head...
A kick was delivered;

that delicate woman fainted from that blow and the force of the poison. When the minister Pracaṇḍa began to look at her, he saw her fallen motionless upon the ground, and this thought occurred to him: "She is dead; I shall leave now."
Then, thinking "Let no one see me," he leaped over the wall and entered Rājagṛha by another path;
having entered it, he gave orders to the king's men.
"Go and inspect the park of the caravan leader Divākara.
They set out.
[21] The youth Suvarṇavarṇa, having departed from Rājagṛha, arrived at his own park.
There he saw the maiden Kāśisundarī, dragged here and there, with her hair disheveled, motionless, and fallen upon the ground. Upon seeing this, a great sense of spiritual urgency arose within him.
He perceived that she must have been brought here and slain by some wicked person of merciless heart, who has abandoned the world beyond and is bound by enmity.

"Fie! Alas! How is it that there are even such beings who strike mercilessly at a woman of such a kind? He searched the entire park, but seeing nothing, he thought to himself: "This well-known woman must have been killed here in this park."
"I see nothing at all here;
in every way, some wicked soul, manifesting his own inherent wickedness, has let fall this thunderbolt of infamy upon my head.
With his mind thus agitated, he stood lost in thought, resting his cheek upon his hand.
Sva Roy 50,5–52,3 [22]: Those royal officers arrived;
having entered that park, they began to search it.
When they saw the maiden Kāśisundarī dragged here and there, with disheveled hair, motionless, and fallen upon the ground,
no one could discern that she was fainted due to the power of the maturation of the former karma of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa.
They thought, "She has simply fainted."
"But rather, she has passed away.
Then those royal officers said to one another,
"Sirs, this woman has been killed by someone."
They searched that entire park,
but seeing no one else except for the youth Suvarṇavarṇa,
they questioned the youth Suvarṇavarṇa.
"Prince, by whom was this woman killed?
He replied, "Gentlemen, I too do not know; I too have seen her only just now."
[23] Then those royal officers began to consult with one another: "Sirs, this prince is exceedingly disciplined; such an act is not possible for him.
We see no other person here at all; we have entered into a state of extreme peril in every respect."
"How should we proceed in this matter?
Thereupon, one of them said,
"Gentlemen, we are not capable of making a decision."
"Let us take this woman and the boy to the hall of justice; there the ministers themselves will decide the matter.
Then those royal officers, having placed the woman upon a palanquin and taken the golden-colored boy, went to the hall of justice.
And there in the hall of justice, the minister Pracaṇḍa, by his very conduct, [was surrounded] by litigants who were favorable [to him].
He sat down together with them;
having assembled, he was waiting primarily for those very royal officers, and when they were seen by him from afar,
he asked them, "Sirs, what is this?"

They reported: "This woman was seen by us dead in the park of the caravan leader Divākara; we searched that park thoroughly, but we saw no one else except for the gold-colored youth. And this youth was questioned by us:
'By whom was this woman killed?'"
"He has said, 'Sirs, I too do not know; by me also this was seen exactly in this way.
Therefore, let the masters now investigate this for themselves."
[24] The minister Pracaṇḍa said, "Sirs,
wait for a moment while I inform the king.
He went to the house of King Ajātaśatru and asked the gatekeeper, "Sir, what is the king doing?"

Therefore, he was told that [the prince], having gone to the upper terrace of the palace, was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with instrumental music performed by women alone. Having gained his favor, he sent a female door-keeper, saying, "Go and inform the King:
the ministers report that the maiden Kāśisundarī has been murdered in the garden by the son of the caravan leader Divākara."
But he would not accept it, saying, "How are we to proceed in this matter?
She went and informed the king; the king, who was exceedingly skilled in amorous play, said:
"Go and say this to the ministers: 'You yourselves must investigate this thoroughly.
Having departed, she reported to the minister Pracaṇḍa: "Thus does His Majesty command."
[25] Then the minister Pracaṇḍa, having come to the hall of justice, said to those royal officers:
"Go, sirs, and summon the executioners.
Summoned by them, the minister Pracaṇḍa spoke to the executioners.
"Sirs, this prince has murdered the maiden Kāśisundarī in the park.

Go, bind the hands of this man of evil conduct tightly behind his back, and while the harsh-sounding drum is being beaten, proclaim his crime at the crossroads, the marketplaces, the squares, and the thoroughfares; then lead him out through the southern city gate."

"Take him to the great cemetery, impale him on a stake, and once he is dead, place him upon the same funeral pyre as the maiden Kāśisundarī and cremate them both. Then those executioners, beholding the youth Suvarṇavarṇa— who was exceedingly handsome and radiant with supreme splendor like the peak of a mountain of refined gold— were deeply moved with agitation.
They said to one another:
"Sirs, although we are executioners, how could we kill such a distinguished man whose sight is so exceedingly rare?
Under no circumstances, even at the cost of our own lives, shall we ever kill him."
[26] When the minister Pracaṇḍa saw them conversing with one another, he asked: "Sirs,
why do you stand here?"
"Lead him here quickly!
They, with palms joined in reverence, began to petition him:
"Be gracious, O Master!"
"Even though we are executioners, we cannot bring ourselves to kill such a distinguished man who is beloved by the great multitude.
The minister Pracaṇḍa, being enraged, said:
"Sirs, if you do not put him to death,"
"Today, your very lives— along with those of your sons, wives, and kinsmen— shall cease to be. Terrified, they said to one another, "Sirs,
this minister’s conduct is inconsistent with justice."
For how could it be that he who is prepared to abandon the youth Suvarṇavarṇa— a distinguished man whose sight is so exceedingly rare— would instead slay us along with our sons, wives, and kinsmen?
We have entered into a most perilous strait.
"How should we proceed in this matter?"—this thought arose in those who were terrified by the fear of death:
"This prince is beloved by the great multitude; therefore, let us first bring him down into the street."
"It is possible that the great multitude itself will set him free;
for who would be able to remain indifferent while he is being executed?
Having said this, they approached his side.
"Let us bind his arms behind his back.

But having beheld him thus resplendent with the perfection of his physical beauty and majesty, they were unable to touch him; consequently, their limbs trembling and their throats choked with tears, they began to wail.
"Alas, what misery! Even we, who are doers of evil deeds, are being employed in such a task as this!
[Sva Roy 61,4–64,2] Then, they were again commanded harshly by the minister Pracaṇḍa: "Why do you delay?"
Terrified, they approached him;
with eyes flooded with tears and trembling, they seized him and bound his arms behind his back with that very gold-yellow garment.
Seeing him thus bound tightly with his arms behind his back, everyone released the fierce minister.

The multitude of people gathered in the execution pavilion, their mental continuums melted by the grief of separation from him, began to shed tears, crying out, "Alas, what a tragedy! From this very moment, the prince, whose sight is so difficult to obtain, will no longer exist!
Then, those executioners brought him down into the street; in the meantime, a great clamor arose, which—

And having heard the clamor, the multitude of people residing in Rājagṛha— including women, men, boys, and girls— as well as those who had arrived from various directions and countries, gathered together.
Beholding the youth Suvarṇavarṇa with his arms tightly bound behind his back, their minds were deeply agitated, and they began to ask in great alarm:
"Sirs, what is this?
Then those executioners, their throats choked with tears and sobbing, said:
"Sirs, it is said that this prince has killed the maiden Kāśisundarī; he has been abandoned for execution and is being proclaimed at the thoroughfares, streets, crossroads, and junctions."
"Before long, he will be led to the great cemetery and executed.
Upon hearing this, that great multitude of people, struck by the pain of separation from him, began to cry out loudly with a single voice.

Alas, alas! How can this prince—so handsome, beautiful, and pleasing; endowed with all major and minor limbs; possessed of a magnificent complexion like refined gold; captivating the minds and eyes of all people; wise, disciplined, gentle, capable, compassionate, high-minded, desirous of the Dharma, and affectionate toward sentient beings—be put to death?
Have the virtuous vanished? Has the Dharma disappeared? Has the sovereignty and dominion of unrighteousness alone now arisen without rival?
Alas, what a tragedy! O sirs, having repeatedly beheld him who was adorned with the most excellent perfections of form and beauty, we formerly experienced supreme delight. (1)
Now, seeing him presided over by executioners, our hearts—overwhelmed by intense grief—are as if bursting;
for he was beloved by the great multitude because of his power to captivate both mind and eye. (2)
How indeed can punishment be inflicted by the king upon her?
How has she—who, though constantly being gazed upon, never brings satiety to embodied beings—been abandoned for execution? Today the ministers have abandoned all compassion. (3-4)
How can such an offense as this be possible for one whose conduct, endowed with humility, is renowned like that of a sage? Alas!
Unrighteousness is awake, while righteousness is either asleep or dead.

That such a separation has now befallen him, despite his being possessed of such virtues; (6) for this is exceedingly dear to women. There, some women, struck by the pain of separation from him, were rolling and tossing about upon the ground.
Some beat their breasts;
some fell into a state of unconsciousness;
each one there experienced the pain of separation as if it were the loss of her own son.
The populace residing in the city of Rājagṛha, that great-souled one who was beloved by the masses, for the most part being struck by the pain of separation from him, began to wail;
the city of Rājagṛha was known to be in a state of utter agitation, trembling as it were, being struck by the grief of separation from him.
[Sva Roy 67,4–69,1 [30]] A young girl emerged from the house of the caravan leader Divākara onto the street.
She heard this account; thereupon, weeping and beating her breast, she went very quickly to her home.
She approached the mother of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, and having approached, she threw herself before her.
Then the mother of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, being terrified, asked:
"Girl, what are you saying?"
Crying out loudly, she began to say:
"Noble lady, Prince Suvarṇavarṇa has been bound tightly behind the back with a cord and is being guarded by executioners.

Without even investigating the claim that the maiden Kāśisundarī was killed in this park, he has been abandoned for execution and is being proclaimed through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions."
"In no long time at all, he will be led to the great cremation ground and executed.
Upon hearing this, Suvarṇavarṇa’s mother, struck by intense grief, fainted and fell to the ground.

Then, her life-breaths restored by the sprinkling of water, she rose up, crying out "O son! O son! while tearing at her hair, beating her breast, trembling, and falling into a swoon again and again. Having departed from her home and entered the street, struck by the grief of separation from her son and with a distracted heart, she lamented this and that, questioning each person she met.
"By which path will the golden-colored boy have been led? Alas, my little son! I do not see you! Save me, save me! Show me my little son!
Thus she cried out as she stood in the middle of the street.
[Sva Roy 70,3–73,3] [32] Just as the caravan leader’s wife did not see the boy Suvarṇavarṇa,
so too, struck by ever-increasing grief and suffering, she cried out loudly, fell at each of his feet, joined her palms, and made this request:
"Save me! Save me! Quickly grant me passage before the prince passes by this way.

My dear son, the golden-colored prince, is being led along this path; you ought to show me favor so that I may see him. And finding no passage there, she cried out, "Alas! Oh, my son, why do I not find [you]?"
She threw herself upon the ground on all fours;
then, like a fish pulled from the water, she began to roll and turn about upon the earth,
and like a female osprey whose young has been snatched away, she wailed most piteously.
Like a cow that has lost its calf, she lamented with many kinds of lowing cries:
"Alas, my little son!
Alas, my beloved!"
Delightful! O beloved!
O agreeable one!
Alas, you who were obtained through hundreds of aspirations!
Alas, you who are handsome, beautiful to behold, and inspiring!
Alas, you who are endowed with all major and minor limbs!
Alas, you who are endowed with an abundance of complexion like the color of refined gold!
Alas, you who captivate the minds and eyes of all people!
Alas, you who are beloved by all people!
Alas, you who bring joy to the eyes!
Alas, O learned, disciplined, confident, charming, and skillful one!
Alas, O compassionate one, lover of the Dharma, and friend to all beings!
Alas, my illuminator of the family! Alas, my son, the lamp of the lineage!
Alas, my beloved of the heart!
Alas, my all-in-all of the heart! Alas, my collection of essences!
Alas, the nectar for my eyes!
"Alas, my bond of affection! Alas, my entire store of merit!
Alas, how is he being led away to his execution like one who is helpless, without even being investigated?"
Once again, with her hands joined in supplication, she addressed the citizens,
speaking with a distressed heart:
"Alas! I am destroyed, joyless; what is this that happens to me?
Is this a dream, or delusion, or perhaps a derangement of the mind?
Thus the virtuous woman, her mind overwhelmed by the intense grief for her son, [lamented]. 1.
Crying out again and again, she informed the citizens:
"He is neither ill-mannered nor ugly, nor is he anything other than dear to my heart;
yet you look on with indifference while my son is being led away. (2-3)
If you have compassion, or if you have partiality toward virtues,
O citizens, act in such a way for me that I may see my son;
he has not been anointed today by me with ointments such as sandalwood.
Nor was he adorned in many ways with drops of yellow pigment on his limbs;
nor was he decorated by me with ornaments such as bracelets and the like.
Nor was he embraced with confidence, nor was he kissed many times. (5–6)
"He did not circumambulate me today, nor did he offer me homage;
how indeed can my son be led away thus?
O, all directions are empty to me today, and my body trembles."
My heart burns and my mind falls into delusion;
8/ led with the utmost haste by cruel executioners, [he cries:
"Alas, alas! I shall never again behold my son, the darling of my heart! 9/

Surely a terrible sin was committed by me in another life, because of which I am thus consumed by grief for my son, like dry grass by fire. By that truth, may my mind never turn toward evil, even toward enemies. (10)
"By that truth, may my son be released from this calamity.
(11) And the caravan leader Divākara, having successfully completed his voyage from the ocean, arrived at Rājagṛha.
As he was entering the city of Rājagṛha, he beheld inauspicious omens;
his heart began to tremble, his limbs began to grow weak,
his eye began to throb, and birds began to shriek harshly before him.
Skilled in omens and well-versed in the cries of birds, he began to reflect:
"Since I perceive these omens as unfavorable, surely a great calamity will befall Prince Suvarṇavarṇa today.
For these signs indicate his separation [from me]," and he said:
Just as my eye throbs and just as the bird cries out, surely a separation from my little son has now arrived;
for my limbs grow weary and my heart trembles. (1)
"Surely today a terrible separation from my son has arrived.
Thus, contemplating hundreds of thousands of such calamities, his limbs and members were sinking with despair.
Trembling and with faltering steps, he somehow managed to enter the royal palace and heard the sound of a great multitude wailing.

Following that sound of lamentation, he descended into the street and saw a great crowd of people crying out, struck by the sorrow of separation as if the city were being ravaged by a *rākṣasa*. A certain man who came face to face with him was questioned by him.
"O man, what is this?
He did not know that this very person was the caravan leader Divākara;
he replied, "The son of the caravan leader Divākara is a youth named Suvarṇavarṇa, who is exceedingly endowed with the perfection of beauty and other virtues."

"It is said that the maiden Kāśisundarī was killed by him in the park. Without even investigating this, he was abandoned for execution and proclaimed with a loud voice through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions:
"Before long, he shall be led to the great cemetery and executed."
Having heard that, the caravan leader Divākara, struck by the pain of separation from his son, suddenly fainted and fell to the ground.

Then, having regained consciousness through the sprinkling of water, he rose up; with the lotus of his face overflowing with waves of tears, he looked about in agitation, wondering, "Alas, by which path has the youth Suvarṇavarṇa been taken?"
Setting out very hurriedly through the middle of the street,
he saw his wife with her hair disheveled, beating her breast with both hands,
wailing with a cry of distress, and experiencing a pain born of separation from her son— intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant.
And having seen her experiencing such pain, his throat choked with intense grief and his eyes overflowing with tears,
he approached her.

[36] Seeing him, she was struck by the even more intense thorns of grief; her lotus-like face filled with waves of surging tears, she rose up in great agitation and very hurriedly threw herself before him.
Then, as she was crying out with a piteous voice, the caravan leader Divākara embraced her and raised her up.
She fell at his feet and said,
"Sārthavāha, save me, save me! Grant me the boon of a son," and she added,
"Comfort me now, for I am ill-fated and joyless."
Weeping and deeply distressed as she is being separated from her son—
O Lord, that very beloved son at whose birth you experienced supreme joy is now being led away for execution. (1–2)

Disciplined, gentle, skillful, and learned in many treatises, your son is a scholar whose beauty is beyond compare; yet he is being led away. Your family lineage will be severed and the pillar of your clan will be broken. (3)
The glorious light that illuminates your lineage is being extinguished.
This, which is the very essence of your heart, this bond of affection,
this nectar for the eyes of men— this is being led away by the executioners.
For all this is being done; this eye is being destroyed, and the heart called "son" is being torn out and carried away.
Therefore, make haste and exert effort for the sake of the son's liberation. (6)
"Even by giving away everything I possess today, deliver my son and me!
May your intentions be fulfilled; may your heart's desire be realized!
Indeed, I shall see that little son of yours alive. (7-8)

[Sva Roy 83,5 – 86,87] [37] Then the caravan leader Divākara, although struck by the sorrow and suffering of separation from his son, maintained his composure and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the citizens:
"O citizens, listen! How indeed is it fitting for you to neglect this calamity that has befallen me?

How is it that, as if in a wilderness, my son—who possesses radiant virtues—is being led away to his execution through the very center of the city without hesitation, even while you all look on? Why do you remain so indifferent?"
"Why is a remedy not considered?
Why do you not strive for the release of the prince?
They replied, "Caravan leader, this prince is so virtuous that this calamity belongs to you alone; rather, it belongs to all of us. However, we see no means for the release of the prince."
"For what reason do we remain here with such dejected minds?
The caravan leader Divākara replied, "Gentlemen, you already know this prince; he is exceedingly compassionate, a great soul, a lover of the Dharma, and affectionate toward all beings."
Even his mind is not capable of conceiving such an improper act, much less committing it;
therefore, let an effort be made for the sake of examining the prince.
If the prince is examined, he will certainly be liberated from this calamity.

And since you are virtuous and common to all people, no fault whatsoever is seen in those who address you; rather, compassion is shown toward me, and your virtue and love for excellence are made manifest.
"Having summoned a mind of compassion, go and inform the king or his ministers;
for perhaps, because they are intent on their own interests, they will not accept your well-reasoned words otherwise.
And I am utterly tormented by the separation from my son."
"Therefore, even by giving away my entire fortune, you must show such favor that the prince may be investigated.
That caravan leader was well-known and had made many friends.

Because of their words and out of affection for the prince’s virtues, they agreed; they then dispatched experienced city merchants to the royal court and said to them, "If the prince is investigated more thoroughly today, we too shall grant the king one hundred thousand gold pieces.
Thereupon, those city merchants arrived at the hall of justice and were seen from afar by the minister Pracaṇḍa, who asked them, "Sirs, what is the purpose of your visit?"

They reported: "The citizens residing in Rājagṛha make this representation: since this Prince Suvarṇavarṇa is exceedingly dear to the people because of his endowment with such excellence of beauty and nobility, the populace living in Rājagṛha will suffer great distress at being separated from him."

Because he is devoted to the Dharma and endowed with virtues such as discipline, no one believes that he has committed this offense. Therefore, we shall grant him a hundred thousand pieces of gold. Furthermore, by our request, let the caravan leader Divākara restore Prince Suvarṇavarṇa and have him investigated once again with even greater care; for if this is done, our request will be fulfilled in its entirety.
It is accomplished;
and the treasury of the king is increased.
[39] Having heard this, the minister Pracaṇḍa became enraged and said:

"Sirs, why is that which was not previously investigated now being investigated again? And as for what you say—that the royal treasury is being increased—how then shall we increase the royal treasury with wealth acquired through unjust means?"
Furthermore, you have not understood the King’s intention.
In every way, you must certainly desire to bring harm to this king through the agency of the people of Vaiśālī, since by such a means you wish to utter dispraise of him,
saying, "The king acts unjustly, for he destroys the countryside without due deliberation."
He rebuked them.

Having rebuked them, he summoned four men who were like the agents of Death (kṛtāntapuruṣa), whose deeds were exceedingly fierce, whose mental continuums had been rendered pitiless through constant practice, and who were devoid of compassion; having summoned them, he said to them:
"Go quickly and take charge of the executioners!

And by my command, you must say to them: 'Quickly lead him out of the city and execute him according to the prescribed method. Furthermore, he must not be released by you at the request of anyone, whether it be me or the king."
"For those who act thus, there will be welfare; otherwise, I shall impose a great bond of transgression upon you.
"So be it, Master," those royal officers replied to him, and with swords in hand, they set out.

[40] Those executioners, creating hundreds of distractions, slowly and gradually led the golden-colored prince through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, proclaiming it as they paraded him about: "Oh, alas! Will there be some who will deliver the prince? Perhaps we shall not commit such an evil deed!"
Those royal officers, with sharp swords in hand, arrived and reported to those executioners exactly what had been commanded.
They said, "If you do not quickly lead him out of the city and execute him according to the prescribed method,
we shall have you executed this very moment."

Seeing those men, who were close to being drenched with water and held swords in their hands like the messengers of Yama, they were terrified; struck with the fear of death, they began to think: "Alas, what a tragedy! No one has come to the prince's rescue;
now he must surely be executed by us ourselves."
Supervised by those royal officers whose eyes were flooded with tears, they began to lead Suvarṇavarṇa out of the city.
Seeing him being led out from the city, many hundreds of thousands of living beings began to cry out in a single voice at the top of their lungs: "Alas, what a tragedy! This is he!"
Divākara the caravan leader is deprived of all his possessions;
this maternal lineage of Divākara the caravan leader is severed;
this lamp of the family of Divākara the caravan leader is extinguished.
This joy of the house of the caravan leader Divākara is being led away to his death;
this crest-jewel of the family of the caravan leader Divākara is being carried off;
this eye of the caravan leader Divākara is being extinguished.
This ornament of the merchant Divākara’s lineage is being stolen;
this heart of the merchant Divākara is being torn out;
these very personified life-breaths of the merchant Divākara are being carried away.
Alas, what a tragedy! How is it that the prince was driven away while wandering thus in the wilderness, and no one has come to his rescue?
Now, like the moon being swallowed by Rāhu, he is being seized from the city of Rājagṛha;
like the sun in the sky over the city of Rājagṛha, he is setting.
This nectar for the eyes of the citizens dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha is being placed beyond the range of vision;
this bond of affection for the citizens dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha is being destroyed;
this ornament of the citizens dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha is being taken away.
This crest-jewel of the citizens dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha is being carried away;
this beloved of the hearts of the citizens dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha is being led to his destruction.
Whom now will the citizens dwelling in Rājagṛha gaze upon with unblinking eyes?
"Seeing whom now will they become joyful in mind?"—thus they became despondent.
Sva Roy 96,5–99,2 [42]: Another man, having come from the minister Pracaṇḍa, reported:
"The prince Suvarṇavarṇa has been expelled from the city of Rājagṛha."
Having heard this, he became joyful in mind.
Then those merchants from the city, having heard it, became despondent; they returned and reported this matter in detail to the citizens.
Having heard that, those citizens also became despondent.
Agitated, they said to one another:
"Sirs, even such a father—a righteous king who ruled according to the Dharma—has been deprived of life by King Kali.
Now he has begun to execute even such distinguished men, whose virtues are renowned, who are beloved by the great multitude, and who are rarely seen."
"Alas, what cruelty! Alas, what ignorance of virtue!

Alas, what lack of discernment on the part of the ministers! For how can this very person—a virtuous and distinguished individual who, being endowed with such extreme beauty and nobility as well as discipline, truly deserves honor—be abandoned for execution without due deliberation?"
"Or rather, such a time has arrived that the wicked flourish;
thus will there come to be such a separation for a person endowed with such virtues.
Proclaiming the wickedness of Time’s oppression, they related this matter in detail to the caravan leader Divākara.
[43] Having heard that, the caravan leader Divākara, his hopes shattered and struck by the intense pain of grief, fainted and fell to the ground. Then,
having regained consciousness through the sprinkling of water, he became despondent in mind and joyless, thinking, "Now my dear son is being executed."
He began to cry out loudly:
"O delight of my eyes! Alas, my son! Alas, the ornament of my family! O father, you who leave me without a protector, you are being cast down upon me, whose fortune is wretched! (1)
My heart is bewildered and the directions now spin before me;
alas, my mind, scorched by the fire of separation from you, is consumed.
[This is the case] for one who is learned, disciplined, and devoted to compassion.

Alas! O dear son, how has such a terrible calamity befallen you? Having attained incomparable joy produced by your birth, O virtuous son, I have fallen once again into the fire of grief through separation from you.
"Alas, how pitiless and lacking in discernment are the ministers of this king, by whom you, my son, endowed with such discipline, were not even considered!
Alas, that monarch has manifested utter cruelty! 5.
"O son, since you have been abandoned today by one such as I without due reflection—
alas, the excellence of virtuous people has surely set within my heart,
for even though you are possessed of merit, O son, you are being executed without anyone to cry out for you."
Have all the deities of this city departed?
For they look on with indifference while such a virtuous person is being slain.
Even the gods, including Indra and the world-protectors, as well as those of great supernatural power—
"Out of compassion, may they protect my son!
(9) May those great-souled sages who now exist, having perfected their vows, protect my son, placing compassion foremost. (10)
[44] The thought occurred to him: "For what purpose do I despair? Suppose I were to call to mind the Blessed Buddha, the sole kinsman of the entire world, the Great Compassionate One;
for that Blessed One is the protector of those who are without a protector."
A protection for those without protection,
a refuge for those without refuge,
and a final resort for those without a final resort.
For indeed, by that Blessed One, many beings who had fallen into hardship, distress, and peril were liberated from those various great fears.
Likewise, merchants who had entered the great ocean and were terrified by the fear of the *makara* were rescued from that fear of death by the mere act of recollecting him.
Similarly, his own mother, who was being slain by the man-eater Aṅgulīmāla—who acted with singular impetuosity and held a raised weapon—was rescued from the fear of the severance of life.

And so, due to the power of the persistence of enmity from a previous birth, a forest-dweller named Hastaka, who was standing near that forest, rescued from the fear of death a yakṣa who had been brought there for food. That yakṣa was one who, by the force of his connection with the enmity of former lives, had set ablaze a cruel fire for the purpose of slaughtering many hundreds of thousands of living beings; whose tongue was licking the saliva flowing from his mouth out of greed for the taste of human flesh; and whose face was terrifyingly hideous with fierce, long, sharp fangs.
"That Blessed One is capable of liberating my son from this peril.
What if I were now to call to mind that very Blessed One, who is supremely compassionate and whose nature is most affectionate?
He then asked a certain lay follower standing nearby, "Where does the Blessed One dwell at present?"
Then that lay follower, recollecting the Blessed One, spoke with a voice faltering and choked with tears:
"O Caravan Leader, you who are the caravan leader of the world, you who bestow happiness upon the world..."
That Great Teacher, the sole kinsman of the entire world, has entered into final peace (nirvṛta).
He who was a lamp for those without a lamp, he who was a refuge and the ultimate resort—
that Jina, the lamp of the world, has entered into final peace through the exhaustion of his oil.

[45] Having heard that, the caravan leader Divākara, struck by the arrow of grief doubled by separation from the Blessed One, fainted and fell to the ground. Then, his life-breath restored by the sprinkling of water, he rose and, facing the direction in which the Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, began to cry out loudly.
Alas, O Dharmarāja, omniscient one, destroyer of the host of enemies that are the defilements!
Having abandoned these helpless people, why have you departed, O Lord of the World?
Alas, O All-pervading One, whose conduct is renowned, sole kinsman of all sentient beings!
O you who are unattached to all worldly unions and who teach the path to Nirvāṇa!
Alas, how indeed will this world, its eyes shrouded by ignorance, wander through cyclic existence deprived of you as its Protector? (2–3)

When you, who are heroic in compassion for others, have attained final nirvana, this world will indeed be without a protector; whom will it rely upon as its lord? And those sons of the people to be trained, who were born from you through the Dharma—
Deprived of you, where will they all find refuge?
O destroyer of suffering, having fulfilled the hopes of many, you have now shattered the hopes of those people; O Sage, where have you gone?
If the citizens should assemble, eager to hear your words—who indeed will now proclaim the True Dharma once you have passed into nirvāṇa?
Alas! This other world, including its gods and kinnaras, is destroyed.
O Sage, since they are now separated from you, their exceedingly rare protector,
how indeed will those living beings who long for the Dharma act—
those who love the teaching, having heard of the parinirvāṇa of you, their sole lord? (8–9)

Having relied upon you, who are steadfast, whose sole essence is compassion, and who are full of pity, what further virtues could anyone not proclaim? Indeed, how could one fail to do so after you have generated great compassion for the sake of the three worlds? (10)
O compassionate one, knower of the truth of the world, you have indeed resorted to equanimity!
Alas! O you who are rich in the jewels of virtue and concentrated for ten million eons, having reached the abyss of death, the ship of Dharma has been cast down. 11–12.
"Alas! How painful it is that this world, blinded by ignorance and deprived of the Buddha as its guide, will perish, lost in the wilderness of rebirth.
Oh, a great decline for the worlds has indeed arrived! (13)
Now that they are separated here from the great jewel of the Buddha,
how is it that the hearts of the wise do not shatter upon seeing the assembly of monks made empty by you, like a herd of cattle deprived of its bull? (14–15)
Whose dust, placed upon the tips of their feet by the gods whose heads are bowed in devotion, will they now bear upon their own heads?
Alas, this impermanence, though equal toward all beings, is indeed cruel. (16)
By you, who even today show no partiality even toward yourself—
by you, the Greatly Compassionate Teacher, the King of Physicians, who treats the disease of the afflictions with the medicine of the Eightfold Path, has been struck down. (17–18)

Alas! How cruel and too soon has the Leader of the World passed away—he who was the unsurpassed giver of sight to this world that had become blind. Now that you have passed into nirvana, who will protect my innocent jewel of a son today?
"Having come here, he will suddenly liberate me while I am being slain.
But now that you, the protector of the helpless, have gone to the supreme destination, alas, I am born today utterly hopeless for my son's life. (20-21)
"Today that which was spoken by you, the Great-Souled One, has been well-fulfilled for me:
that the separation from all beloved ones occurs—this is the most excellent word.
[46] Having lamented in this way in many ways, he said to that lay follower:
"O sir, does even some great disciple remain of that Blessed One?
To whom has the Blessed One entrusted his teaching before passing into parinirvāṇa?"
Then that lay devotee said: "Caravan leader, it is heard that the Blessed One, having entrusted the teaching to the Elder Mahākāśyapa, has entered final nirvāṇa;

and the Elder Mahākāśyapa also, by the very command of the Blessed One, having entrusted the teaching to the Elder Ānanda, has entered final nirvāṇa. Now this great-souled Elder Ānanda is the bearer of the burden of the teaching."
Now, like a Tathāgata, out of compassion he travels to various villages, cities, towns, hamlets, and market towns, performing acts of grace for those people who are to be disciplined.
Thus, he plants roots of virtue in sentient beings who have not yet planted them,
and he brings to maturity the continuum of virtue in those in whom it has already been gathered.
He brings liberation to those whose continuums of roots of virtue are fully ripened.
Likewise, like a skilled physician, he provides the medicine of the teaching of the Dharma to cure sentient beings afflicted by the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Like the sun, he dispels the darkness of the afflictions for sentient beings overwhelmed by the darkness of the afflictions by means of the mass of rays from the teaching of the true Dharma.
Like the moon, he awakens the groves of white water-lilies that are those to be trained by means of his assembly of eloquent speech;
like a universal monarch, he instructs thousands of minor kings who are those to be trained through the teaching of the True Dharma;
and like a lion, he puts to flight the herds of deer that are the followers of false teachers with the roar of his own wisdom and inspired eloquence.
Like a guide, he brings to completion those who are to be trained through his instructions;
like a caravan leader, he causes them to enter the hand of the True Dharma;
and like a great cloud, he causes the seeds of virtue to sprout.
Like a mother and father, he provides instruction on what is beneficial and what is harmful;
he tames beings who are untamed, liberates those who are unliberated, consoles those who are unconsoled, and leads to final nirvana those who have not yet attained it.
Likewise, he delivers beings who have fallen into hardship, distress, and peril from great fears.
"In brief, that Great Being performs the work of a Buddha;
remember him alone.
He is capable of liberating your son today from this peril."
Having heard this, the caravan leader Divākara, as if his life had returned after having departed, spoke with agitation to that lay follower:
"Where does Ānanda dwell now?"
He said, "Caravan leader, I have heard that the Elder Ānanda is currently staying in Vaiśālī at the Āmrapālī grove.

Then the caravan leader Divākara rose suddenly, placed his knees upon the ground, and bowed with palms joined toward Vaiśālī; struck by the sorrow and pain of separation from his son, the lotus of his face was overflowing with waves of tears.
With eyes clouded by tears, he began to entreat the Elder Ānanda with intense devotion.
If you, O Supreme Teacher, are the most excellent knower of the dispositions of sentient beings, then having understood their intentions and latent tendencies, listen to this request:
The Blessed Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, as have his disciples of great supernatural power.
For you alone remain among them as the one who increases the teaching.
You have become the source of consolation for this world; you are its ultimate refuge.
Now, you must look upon the task that brings benefit to all sentient beings.
Therefore, while such a protector as you stands here as our guardian,
how can our son— who has no one else to cry out to— be thus put to death?
If there were no concern for the welfare of sentient beings, those like you would not remain [in this world].
How can you thus disregard this person who is being slaughtered at a *śrāddha*?
O you of excellent vows, if you indeed maintain this body for the sake of sentient beings, then,
turning toward compassion, look upon my son.
Lift me up, along with my wife, who am now without remedy, unprotected, without refuge, and mired in the mud of grief;
to whom else shall I appeal, for who else is thus devoted to the welfare of the world? (7)
It was pointed out by Śākyamuni, O Lord, just as it is now for you:
"O All-pervading One, since there is no other protector for my son but you, you ought to come quickly and save my son. (8–9)
"Seized by the unbearable and evil-souled enemy that is grief for my son, I am joyless along with my wife; O Ānanda, gladden me today! (Sva Roy 118,4–121,122)

[48] Then, in the meantime, the Elder Ānanda, being filled with compassion and reflecting, surveyed the world with the eye of a disciple three times during the night and three times during the day, considering: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms? Who is headed for the lower realms?"
"Whom shall I lift up from the path of ruin and establish in heaven and liberation?
To whom, sunk in the mire of sensual desire, shall I grant a hand to pull them out?
Whom, destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereignty and mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?"—thus did the Elder Ānanda perceive.

With an eye equal to that of the Elder Śāradvatīputra, having seen the youth Suvarṇavarṇa— who had accumulated a vast store of roots of merit— fallen into such hardship, distress, and peril, he remained right where he was and, by means of his supernatural power, extended forth an arm like the trunk of an elephant, and suddenly [reached] King Ajātaśatru, who was staying on the upper terrace of the palace and living in extreme negligence.
Awakening him with the sound of a snap of the fingers, he spoke in a resonant voice:

"Great King, you have not acted wisely, since you did not personally investigate the matter regarding the youth Suvarṇavarṇa. Therefore, it is not right that he—though innocent—is now being led out from Rājagṛha to the great cemetery to be executed."

"Stop this! Having heard these words of the Elder Ānanda, the king, filled with agitation, quickly bowed to the Elder Ānanda and, rising while still in the upper white palace, cried out in a loud voice toward the four quarters: "Listen! Whoever, having gone swiftly to the great cemetery, shall [protect] the youth Suvarṇavarṇa from being executed according to my command—"

"I shall release him and bestow upon him a golden casket and five excellent villages. Hearing these words of the king, that prince was beloved by the great multitude, and thousands of living beings ran forth.
[49] Now, in the meantime, the executioners, supervised by those royal officers, took the boy Suvarṇavarṇa and arrived at the great cemetery.
The maiden Kāśisundarī, adorned by her own kinsmen with garments of blue, yellow, red, and white, was [prepared] upon...
Having placed her upon a litter, she was carried out to the great cemetery; her kinsmen, having set her down in one spot, gathered wood and began to construct a funeral pyre.
Then those executioners said to them:
"This much [wood] must be piled by you upon the funeral pyre;
wait for a moment while we impale the boy Suvarṇavarṇa on a stake and execute him,
for the reason that this boy Suvarṇavarṇa must be placed upon the same funeral pyre as the girl Kāśisundarī and cremated together."
Having said this, they began to set the trident upon the earth.

Then the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, having set his spear upon the ground, looked at the measuring line and called to mind his mother; his heart melted with intense grief, and he began to shed tears, thinking:
"Now that she hears of my separation, what state will my mother be in?"
"For she who previously, even when not seeing me for as little as half a watch, experienced such supreme agony—how will she sustain her life today, separated from me, her only son?
Alas, what a tragedy! Even I am so unfortunate that, on account of me, my mother must experience the suffering of separation from her child.
Then those executioners drove that stake into the earth and began to converse among themselves.
"Who among us is impaling the prince on the stake? Then, each one of them began to make an excuse: "You all must impale him;
a headache afflicts me excessively."
Thinking, "I have a pain in my back," or "I have a pain in my side," not one among them was able to bring himself to do that improper act.
[51] Then, having heard their conversation and seeing the stake driven into the earth, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa thought, "Alas! Now I shall no longer exist.
Agitated by the defects of *saṃsāra*, longing for the path to liberation, and perceiving himself to be joyless, his eyes overwhelmed with supreme fear and despair, he began to cry out:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Having now attained this human state—a most rare festival of the True Dharma—I shall not die until my purpose has been fulfilled. Alas, I shall wander once more in saṃsāra;
once again I shall have to dwell within the prison of cyclic existence."
Again one will have to wander through the wilderness of saṃsāra;
again one will have to enter the great thicket of saṃsāra;
again one will have to fall into the great abyss of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, I shall have to remain in the midst of the great mire of saṃsāra;
furthermore, I shall have to be reborn in the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Pratāpana, Avīci, and other such hells;
and once again, I shall have to be reborn in various wombs as an elephant, a gavaya, a buffalo, a hare, a śarabha, a deer, a ruru, a camara, or a cat.

Furthermore, I shall again have to be reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta) who are constantly overwhelmed by the great suffering and dejection of hunger, thirst, and so forth; for whom even the sound of food and drink has vanished; who subsist on urine, excrement, spittle, snot, and the like; and who suffer from goiters and other such ailments.
And it is heard that at certain times, at certain moments, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas arise in the world;
just as the flower of the udumbara tree appears only at certain times, at certain moments, so too the appearance of the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is made known in the worlds.

The perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to obtain; human birth is difficult to obtain; rebirth in a noble land is difficult to obtain; freedom from impairment of the sense faculties is difficult to obtain; lack of dullness, lack of muteness, and lack of being unable to communicate by hand are difficult to obtain; and the capacity to understand the meaning of teachings that are well-spoken or ill-spoken is difficult to obtain.
And as for me, because of my abstention today, I shall not exist here [in this state] again.
Thus, this human state of mine, freed from the eight inopportune conditions, will go to waste.
Therefore, what shall I do now?
Does the Blessed One, the Buddha of great compassion, still remain, whom I might call to mind while in this condition?

One who is without protector, without refuge, without shelter, without resort, and without light, having fallen into hardship, distress, and confinement— he will come and deliver them because of his great compassion;
yet that Blessed One, due to my own misfortune and transgression, has very quickly entered final nirvāṇa.
"Therefore, why do I now, in this state, still remember?
Who will come out of compassion like the Tathāgata and deliver me?
Having become hopeless, he began to tremble.
[53] The thought occurred to him: "The great-souled Elder Ānanda is staying there;
I shall call him to mind."
That great-souled one is also heard to have a mental continuum whose intent is devoted to the welfare of all sentient beings.
To him the Blessed One and the Elder Mahākāśyapa entrusted the entire teaching.
Therefore, he must now, having repeatedly surveyed [the world], act for the benefit of all sentient beings; he is possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty.
Realizing, "The Elder Ānanda is capable of rescuing me from this calamity; I shall call him to mind," his eyes were flooded with tears of emotion,
and he was agitated by the fear of *saṃsāra*.
Having attained a state of supreme spiritual urgency, he began to entreat the Elder Ānanda with an intense disposition.

O Elder Ānanda, you should now hear my petition, as I am terrified by the fear of saṃsāra and devoid of joy. Having set down the burden of the welfare of sentient beings, the Omniscient One, whose very nature is compassion—
O, when the great-souled Kāśyapa attained final liberation,
that elder Kāśyapa, having accomplished his purpose, passed into parinirvāṇa after entrusting the burden of this world to you alone for its prosperity.

Now that the Perfectly Awakened One, the kinsman of the world, who was dedicated to the welfare of all beings, and the illustrious Kāśyapa have passed into nirvāṇa, you are the protector of the protectorless and the bestower of fearlessness upon those who are afraid. 4.
A place of rest for the weary, a refuge for those seeking refuge;
you must perform the duty of a Teacher, for you are the sole kinsman of the world.
You are the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples, and you are the bearer of the burden of the Teaching.
If you do not lift me out from this abyss of suffering today, I am lost;
for I know of no other protector at present.
I do not fear death as much as I fear that which is certain for one who is born: [the descent into] suffering. (7)
Knowing the way of escape from the ocean of saṃsāra,
yet having obtained this rare moment free from the eight inopportune states, it causes me great anguish that I must die with my purpose unfulfilled. (8–9)
The appearance of the all-seeing Buddhas is indeed rare;
therefore, having come to you, act in such a way that my lineage does not become fruitless.
Your unwavering compassion is known to exist toward all living beings.
Therefore, it is not right for you to neglect me, who yearns for the path to liberation.
And if you, O illustrious one, are devoted to the welfare of all beings,
then look upon me, who have fallen into this state of extreme hardship and distress.
"Thus, having seen with your divine eye that there is no protection,
you ought to come quickly today to rescue me.

[54] Now, in the meantime, the great-souled Elder Ānanda, having girded his loins for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the entire world, and having— out of compassion and with his divine eye, whose mental continuum was affected by beholding the activities of infinite sentient beings— observed the youth Suvarṇavarṇa in this state, his mental disposition was impelled by pity through a divine radiance.

Having illuminated the circle of the world, surrounded by five hundred Arhats, he suddenly ascended into the sky by means of his supernatural power, filling the expanse of the heavens as if with masses of twilight clouds.
With a body shining intensely like a concentrated mass of the splendor of the entire universe, he set out toward the cremation ground.
King Ajātaśatru, stationed above on the white palace, beheld him.
