Seeing the Elder Ānanda approaching toward the great cremation ground, accompanied by a vast community of monks arranged in the shape of a crescent moon, adorning the expanse of the sky with his supernatural power like masses of twilight clouds floating above, he thought to himself: "Surely the Elder Ānanda has come for the sake of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa."

"Having relied upon that, he will desire to teach a Dharma of great wonder and marvel. Thinking thus, "I shall go to the great cemetery," he immediately paid homage to the Elder Ānanda and his retinue, descended very quickly from the roof of the house, and proceeded on foot, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of living beings.

He set out for the great cemetery. In the meantime, the executioners were threatened by those royal officers with raised weapons: "For what reason do you delay? Quickly impale this prince on the stake!
Then those executioners, being terrified, prepared to impale the golden-colored prince upon the stake.
Having said this, they began to cast him out.
Prince Suvarṇavarṇa, his mind distressed by the defects of cyclic existence and having become hopeless, began to cry out:
"Alas, what a tragedy! I have been abandoned by the noble Ānanda; how is it that after taking me into account, he did not protect me?"

[Sva Roy 137,3 – 141,3 [55]] Now, in the meantime, the great-souled Elder Ānanda, approaching from afar, filled all the directions with his pervasive voice and spoke, consoling the gold-colored youth:
"Do not fear, child! It is for the sake of those to be trained like yourself that I bear this body which resembles a venomous serpent.
Therefore, child, do not fear; today I shall deliver you from this peril, and today I shall fulfill the wish of the Blessed Buddha."

Today, I shall make fruitful that very teaching which was entrusted by the Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, who knows and sees—and by the Elder Mahākāśyapa; today I shall manifest the majesty of the foremost disciple;
today I shall fulfill your heart’s desire.
Today I shall remove from you this fear of death and the fear of cyclic existence; today I shall extract the thorn of doubt and idle talk;
today I shall cleanse with the probe of the ointment of knowledge your eyes, which have been clouded by the film of false views.
Today I shall extinguish the fire of your anger;
today I shall clothe you in the state of being free from passion;
today I shall cause the seeds of your virtue to sprout.
Today I lift you out from the mire of saṃsāra; today I ferry you across the ocean of suffering;
today I lead you to the end of the wilderness of saṃsāra.
Today I shall sever your bonds of affliction;
today I shall shatter the door-panel of your hindrances.

Today I will act in such a way that you shall attain the state of an Arhat—the most difficult to obtain throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—through the complete abandonment of all primary and secondary afflictions.
Today you shall burn the entire forest of afflictions with the fire of knowledge;
today your mind shall become free from doubt, O one whose fever has departed.
Today, my child, you shall suddenly cut down the long-standing tree of birth.
With the great vajra of wisdom, you shall thoroughly sever that which is exceedingly difficult to cut.
Having boarded the raft of vigor, you shall today cross over the ocean of existence, with its whirlpools of the waters of passion and pride and its waves of conceit. //2-3//

With the great vajra of wisdom, you shall shatter this mountain of suffering—characterized by birth and enjoyment, marked by old age, and crowded with the caves of death—which for thousands of millions of eons you have not attained. 4. The state that was not found by you throughout thousands of millions of aeons, [you shall now attain].
"Therefore, my child, today you shall attain that which is most difficult to obtain—the state free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

[56] Then, having heard this from the Elder Ānanda, Prince Suvarṇavarṇa was comforted as if his life had returned after departing; his hair stood on end with joy, his gaze was fixed upon the expanse of the sky, and his mind was entirely devoted to the Elder Ānanda.
"So be it. Then those royal officers said to the executioners:
"Sirs, these monks are coming, having plunged into the expanse of the sky."
"These compassionate ones might perhaps come and create an obstacle;
therefore, quickly impale this prince upon the stake,
lest great misfortune befall you due to your transgression of the king's command."
Then those executioners, terrified by the fear of the destruction of their sons, wives, kinsmen, relatives, and their own lives, lifted up the boy Suvarṇavarṇa and began to fix him upon the stake.
Thereupon, the Elder Ānanda suddenly exercised such supernatural power that upon that stake there appeared a large lotus of vast proportions with a wide pericarp, rivaling the orb of the moon;
and upon the pericarp of that lotus, the boy Suvarṇavarṇa sat cross-legged. And...
Beholding him seated cross-legged upon the pericarp of the lotus, many hundreds of thousands of millions of deities situated in the expanse of the sky let out a cry of "Ha! Ha!"—
Oh, the greatness of the Teaching, for it is indeed the marvelous wonder of the Omniscient One!

Even a disciple can thus perform such a miraculous manifestation of a Tathāgata; today, the noble Ānanda has likewise revealed his great majesty with a truly wondrous and sublime power, just like the Sugata himself.

When the sun of the Jina had set, which dispels the darkness of all transgressions, oh, this glorious sun of the Elder Ānanda has now risen! Adorned with the rays of the majesty of his own wisdom-virtues, [he shines forth]. (3)
The Elder Ānandacandra [has illuminated] the sphere of the sky that is the world; the world, which had been shrouded in darkness due to the absence of the Sugata’s light,
has today been perfectly illuminated by the lamp of the noble Ānanda.
When the Jewel of the Buddha, endowed with all inconceivable qualities, had vanished,
the glorious Ārya Ānanda arose as the crest-jewel of the world.

[57] Then the Elder Ānanda, whose radiance surpassed that of the stainless lunar orb of autumn, appearing like the sun veiled by a mass of twilight clouds, his form shining intensely as if he were a concentrated heap of the splendor of the entire world, eclipsing the brilliance of the sun with his own luster,
arrived surrounded by a retinue of five hundred Arhats; while still stationed in the sky, he beheld Suvarṇavarṇa.
He addressed the prince:
"My son, only rarely, at some time or other, do Tathāgatas appear in the world."
The teachers of men and gods, possessing vision and having transcended conflict, proclaim the Dharma that dispels all suffering:
suffering, the origin of suffering, and the overcoming of suffering. //1//
The noble eightfold path, secure and leading to Nirvana;
while this Dharma, which dispels all suffering, is being taught, those who have destroyed ignorance through wisdom do not undergo rebirth again. (2-3)

[58] Immediately after these words, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of self-existence, which rises with twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Then the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, and as if having attained the sovereignty of a universal monarch, was filled with supreme joy and gladness;
remaining right there with palms joined in reverence, he began to praise the Elder Ānanda.
Homage to you, Elder Ānanda; homage to you, supreme among elders! Homage to you, great sage who bears the banner of the sons of the Victors!
Oh, how vast is your compassion; oh, how supreme is your mercy! 1.
It is fitting that the title "Lord of the World" has spread throughout the earth for you, by whom I have been liberated from this great peril;
for I, who was afflicted by fear and without a protector, have been delivered by you as my protector. (2-3)
The moon-like Sage has risen, with the cooling rays of loving-kindness and compassion, to refresh this world scorched by the fires of suffering;
yet that which he has done for me was not accomplished by my mother, nor by my father, nor even by my kinsmen. 4.
Having approached you as a virtuous friend, that which I have obtained—5/ all evil destinies are closed, the gate of liberation is opened;
all oceans are dried up, and the mountains of bones are crossed. 6/
Samsara, which has no beginning, middle, or end, and is crowded with the fears of affliction,
was multiplied by you through even-minded wisdom and established at its limit.
The thorn of views, adhering since beginningless time, has been completely uprooted.
"Having obtained the best of physicians here, I am born into happiness and free from fever. [8] Then,
the deities, having observed the mind of the Elder Ānanda, [arrived] at that very moment at the Great Cremation Ground.

It was cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel; it was laid out, sprinkled with sandalwood water, perfumed with fragrant incense, adorned with raised banners, flags, and archways, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and cords, strewn with most variegated and fragrant flowers, and exceedingly beautiful like the Nandana grove of the gods. And for the sake of the Elder Ānanda, it was constructed with various patterns fashioned from the arrangement of diverse jewels.

A great divine throne made entirely of gold, complete with a footstool, was prepared; likewise, divine seats were prepared for the sake of those five hundred Arhats. Then the Elder Ānanda descended from the sky and sat upon the lion-throne.
Those five hundred arhats also descended and sat down on the prepared seats.

Sva Roy 150,4–153,3 [60]: King Ajātaśatru, accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of living beings, arrived and beheld that splendor and the gold-colored youth, who rivaled the orb of the moon, seated upon a lotus.

Beholding him seated upon the pericarp, like the full moon of autumn released from a mass of clouds, blazing with splendor like a golden sacrificial pillar, his mental continuum was whirled by supreme wonder; his hair stood on end,
his lotus-like face was filled by the surging waves of the highest joy, and his mental continuum was overwhelmed by the force of supreme faith.

He prostrated with his entire body at the feet of the Elder Ānanda; then, having wiped the feet with his snout and risen, he placed both kneecaps upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and looking up at the Elder Ānanda, said:
"Homage to you, O supreme teacher, by whom this very day such a thing has been performed!"
I have personally emerged for the protection of the people.
If I and these people of yours were not taken into account, I would have been destroyed by the thunderbolt-like fall of the Sage’s word of reproach. (1-2)
If you, O Sage, who are devoted to the welfare of all beings, had not been my protector,
I would have been consumed this very day by the forest fire of remorse.
Oh, how great is the power of your wisdom and how supreme is this compassion of yours!
And this wondrous conduct has been perfectly revealed—oh!
Having seen this most marvelous miracle of yours, O blameless one, I have attained supreme tranquility; I do not think even the Tathāgata himself has ever done so.
For this world fallen into hardship, you are the protector, you are the ultimate refuge;
you are the benefactor of all sentient beings, as affectionate as the Blessed One.
The joy that I experienced in the past upon beholding the Blessed One— [that same joy arises now]. 6.
"Beholding you today as the bearer of the banner of the Jina’s teaching.
(7) Then, having thus praised the Elder Ānanda and having risen with a mind filled with supreme joy, that king—

Having approached the vicinity of the stake with the utmost haste, he then extended his hands and, with supreme affection— as if for a beloved son lost and now found— himself lowered the gold-colored youth from that lotus throne, embraced him firmly,
and kissed him repeatedly on the head.
With eyes clouded by tears of joy, gazing at the youth Suvarṇavarṇa with unblinking eyes, he said:
"That pleasure which I felt in former times upon the acquisition of a kingdom did not equal this joy that now increases as I see you released from this peril. (1)
"O son, by good fortune I now behold this lotus-face of yours, which steals the splendor of the full moon and has eyes like the petals of a blue lotus;
it is adorned with the excellence of the qualities of refined complexion and beauty. (2)
Beholding your body, endowed with all its limbs, I gaze upon it.
By what pitiless and evil-minded person has your wickedness been made known, by whom you—so beloved by men—have been abandoned for the sake of slaughter? (3-4)

Whom would this conduct endowed with discipline, these words that bring joy to the ears, and this most wonderful form not delight? Who could have an aversion toward virtues, and who always follows after faults? (5)
Whose heart is like the essence of a diamond, and who is a knower of distinctions?
(6) Surely his heart was made of stone and devoid of consciousness; he has spoken such that you, my son, are not dear to him. (7)
A blazing thunderbolt has been raised to be hurled at my head, or a sharp weapon at my throat, or a firm spear at my chest;
by whom indeed has this ignominious thunderbolt been prepared to be cast down upon me? (8)

Aha! The world, scorched by the sun’s rays of the sharp suffering of separation from the Tathāgata, has been refreshed by the great cloud of the Elder Ānanda with the rain of the nectar of his own words.
Oh, how the aspirations of the Tathāgata have been perfectly fulfilled!
Oh, how the role of helmsman for the Tathāgata’s teaching has been manifested!
Oh, how the state of being a bearer of the Tathāgata’s teaching has been made manifest!
"Aha! The foremost disciple has made his name meaningful.
By this very marvel—through the power of his own greatness of virtue and the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings—he has revealed the greatness of the virtues of the Omniscient One.
Aha! This Great Being has demonstrated his intention to repay the kindness of that Blessed One, the Greatly Compassionate One!"
[77] Then King Śūradatta, his mental continuum overcome by a surge of faith, approached the Elder Ānanda and prostrated himself with his entire body at the Elder Ānanda’s feet.
Having risen and placed both her knees upon the ground, her body bristling with horripilation from joy and her hands joined in reverent salutation, she began to praise the Elder Ānanda:
"Homage to you, O best of men! Homage to you, ocean of learning!
Homage to you, inconceivable and most wonderful upholder of the Victor’s teaching! (1)

Oh, how the majesty of the Buddha’s teaching has been perfectly revealed today by you, who have performed an inconceivable and marvelous benefit for the world! This was accomplished by the Blessed One and by the wise noble Kāśyapa. (2)
The teaching has been entrusted to you; today it has been made fruitful.
By performing this great, most wonderful, and inconceivable benefit for sentient beings, the majesty of the qualities of the Omniscient One is reflected in you today.
"What is surprising if the Perfectly Awakened One has accomplished the welfare of all beings in such a way,
for he is indeed omniscient, all-seeing, and possessed of great compassion?
(5) But this I consider even more surprising— that you, being a disciple..."
"By the Great Compassionate One himself, what a great benefit for sentient beings has been accomplished!
Oh, how well-gained is my gain, as is that of this people of Magadha,
for whom you, ever intent on their welfare, have acted thus even while they were heedless."
"It is fitting that this teaching has been entrusted by the Tathāgata to you,
since today a great and most wonderful deed has been performed by you, just as it was by the Sugata.
Then, the Elder Ānanda was struck with wonder at the greatness of his virtues.
Constantly recollecting the Perfectly Awakened One, he always offered this salutation:
"Homage be to you, O Great Hero, Perfectly Awakened One, supreme among bipeds! You, whose disciple likewise always exerts himself for the welfare of sentient beings. (10)
The Tathāgata has perfectly and loftily revealed his own greatness; we consider this assembly of people to be as if not empty because of you. (11) Sva Roy 211,5 – 213,214

[78] Then the king asked the Elder Ānanda: "Elder, what karma was performed by the caravan leader Divākara together with his wife, as a result of which he has become wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments,
and has also attained the vision of the Truths within the teaching of the Blessed One?"

What karma was performed by the monks Kāśisundara and Pracaṇḍa, such that they were born into a family of great wealth, vast riches, and great enjoyments, and having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions? And what karma was performed by the monk Suvarṇavarṇa?
By the ripening of which karma he has today been born into a family of great wealth and great enjoyment;
thus he is so handsome, beautiful to behold,
and pleasing, endowed with all major and minor limbs, and possessed of an abundance of complexion like the color of refined gold.
Captivating the minds and eyes of all people, his body was draped in garments of golden hue;
from his body wafted the fragrance of sandalwood, and from his mouth the scent of blue lotuses. At his birth, a rain of garments and a rain of karṇikāra flowers fell.

"And those robes were golden-colored; thus, having become one of such great supernatural power and great majesty after going forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions," so said the Elder Ānanda. (Sva Roy 214,1–3) [79]
"O Great King, it is precisely by these [causes] that actions were previously performed in other births; indeed, the fruits of actions ripen for embodied beings."
In the past, O Great King, ninety-one aeons ago, there appeared in the world a Blessed One named Vipaśyin, a Tathāgata,
perfectly endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a Teacher.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, who is the awakened one of gods and humans,
having departed from the royal capital of Bandhumatī, dwells in the Bandhumatīya grove.

[81] Now at that time, in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, there lived a caravan leader named Karṇa, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled Vaiśravaṇa himself.
He was a preeminent family man in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, and he had brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her.

While he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, his wife became pregnant. Meanwhile, the caravan leader Karṇa, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred merchants, set out upon the great ocean.
And as that fetus grew,
so too did whatever wealth Karṇa the caravan leader possessed— whether it was in his storehouse, in his fields, or in other lands— become partly consumed by fire, partly carried off by thieves,
and partly seized by his servants who then fled.
When the caravan leader’s wife reached the full term of her pregnancy, she gave birth to a boy who was black-skinned, extremely deformed,

and whose body was marred by eighteen unfavorable marks; from his body and from his mouth there began to waft such an utterly foul odor that, upon smelling it, the household members residing in that house became utterly repulsed.
As soon as that boy was born, a fire broke out in that house, by which the house and all its wealth were consumed without remainder.
The merchant’s wife somehow managed to take the boy and emerged from that house;
and when that fire, having burnt the house and all the wealth without exception, itself went out.

Then the caravan leader’s wife, having entered that half-collapsed ruined shed, spread out half of her cloak upon the ground, laid the boy down, and, sighing long and hot breaths while recollecting Karṇa the caravan leader, began to weep:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Such a reversal of fortune has come upon me!"

[83] When the female and male slaves, laborers, and servants of the caravan leader Karṇa saw that disaster, they became terrified, thinking, "Let us go, lest we too perish! and having abandoned the wife of the caravan leader Karṇa, they fled.
Thereupon, a certain maidservant reflected:
"I have experienced many kinds of prosperity in the house of the caravan leader Karṇa;
it would not be fitting for me to flee at such a time, abandoning the caravan leader’s wife, who is now helpless and alone."
She alone remained by the side of the caravan leader’s wife;
and all that property of the caravan leader’s wife had been consumed by fire, so that there was not even enough for a single day’s sustenance.
[84] Then that maidservant went to those who were the friends, relations, and kinsmen of the caravan leader Karṇa and said to them, "Sirs,
the wife of the caravan leader Karṇa is in such a state;
please provide her with sustenance."
From the very moment they began to take her in marriage, hundreds of misfortunes appeared within their own families as well.

They perceived: "This son of the merchant Karṇa is extremely inauspicious; by the power of his lack of merit, the entire extent of the merchant Karṇa’s household wealth and prosperity has gone to ruin. Therefore, if we too—"
"We shall provide for his maintenance; before long, such a state will come to pass in our own homes as well, just as it did for the caravan leader Karṇa.
In every way, it is not even proper to utter his name; rather, those maidservants said to that female slave, 'You must no longer enter our dwellings.'"
[85] Having been rebuked by them, she thought:
"Now the wife of the caravan leader has become completely despondent in every respect."
"How should I proceed in this matter? Or rather, since I have taken up this burden, I must now protect the caravan leader's wife all the more.
Thereupon, she went to the houses of others and began to work for wages.
There, she began to support herself, her husband, and the boy by whatever price she obtained;
and because that boy was exceedingly deformed, he was given the name Virūpa.
By chance, that servant girl received a wage that decreased day by day.
Thereupon, those three living beings began to subsist with extreme difficulty.
Sva Roy 222,4–224,5 [86]: The caravan leader’s wife reflected:
"Indeed, I have been abandoned by all my male and female slaves, laborers, servants, friends, kinsmen, and relatives; whatever little life remains to me, it is entirely due to this maidservant."
For she is like a mother to me in her affection;
how long will she continue working alone until she falls into exhaustion,
even while receiving her wages?
"It cannot be sustained by that much alone;

therefore, I too shall experience the consequences of my own karmic transgression and perform work for wages. Having reflected thus, she went with that maidservant to the houses of others and began to perform work for wages; she was exceedingly delicate.
Afflicted by the suffering of hunger and other such pains, she repeatedly fell into a state of delusion while performing her labor.
Then, exhausted and sighing long and hot breaths, she called Karṇa, the caravan leader, to mind and began to weep:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Such a reversal of fortune has come upon me, that I—once the preeminent glory of the entire city—[have now reached this state]."
"I have now experienced, even in this very life, great suffering and dejection as I perform labor for hire in the houses of others, having once been the most excellent woman in the entire city."

[87] And seeing her thus tormented by suffering and weeping, that maidservant began to weep as well: "Alas, what a tragedy! Even in this very life, the wife of a caravan leader—clad in garments from Kāśī, fine and most exquisite, her body adorned with garlands of various fragrant flowers; her cheeks scented with mouth-perfume prepared from many fragrant substances—was like an Apsaras dwelling in the Nandana grove."

Having distributed food, drink, clothing, ornaments, and so forth, as well as female and male slaves, laborers, servants, friends, relatives, and kinsmen, according to their merit— now, in this very life, with head uncovered, limbs smeared with layers of filth, all parts of the body completely withered by the suffering of hunger and other pains, and wearing a tattered, extremely filthy rag that serves as a dwelling for hundreds of lice;

With her waist concealed, having become the lowest of all in the city, she performs labor for hire in the houses of others and experiences great suffering and dejection; oh, what a reversal of fortune!
Oh, how fickle are the riches of sensual enjoyment!
"Oh, how wonderful is the variety of karmas! he said: "She who previously went forth from the entrance of this street like an apsaras, clothed in fine silks and adorned with every ornament—[1]"

Thus, by the reversal of fortune, she who was formerly like a celestial maiden—the very nectar for the eyes of men—has now arrived in such a state; with her limbs scorched by filth, she wears a tattered, frayed rag. (2)

Or, seeing her now as a female ghost (preta), his mind recoils from her very sight. She who was formerly the most excellent woman in the city due to her abundance of wealth has today reached a state of extreme wretchedness, even among the miserable. (3-4)
She who formerly enjoyed great prosperity with joy now, having reached this state, grieves in her suffering. Alas for the wretchedness of saṃsāra! Alas for the impermanence of prosperity! (5)
"How is it that, having been so happy, she has come to be a vessel for suffering?
(6) Then, the caravan leader’s wife, together with that maidservant, began in this sequence to perform work for wages in the houses of others.
And due to the power of Prince Virūpa’s demerit, the price he received diminished day by day;
eventually, at a later time, after making him work until sunset, he obtained nothing at all,
until finally no one would even make him work.
Meanwhile, the caravan leader’s wife began to converse with her maidservant:
"Now not even anyone will make us do work;
we must certainly go about begging for alms."
Taking an alms-bowl, they began to wander for alms.
When Prince Virūpa became capable of wandering about, his mother said to him, "Son, from now on you should eat by wandering for alms yourself.
She gave him an alms-bowl.
Taking that bowl, he entered the street.

Seeing him—so exceedingly dark, with a loathsome complexion, utterly deformed, and his body disfigured by eighteen unfavorable marks—the people became utterly averse to him; they turned their faces away and walked on with heads cast down.
As he approached the door of any house, those [inhabitants], upon smelling that extremely foul odor from his body, would suddenly [turn away].
Having blocked both nostrils and struck him with wood, stones, gravel, and so forth, they drive him out, saying, "Go quickly from here!
Like a living creature, wherever he goes within the mire that extends throughout the city, there he is struck with wood, stones, gravel, and so forth, and driven away.

Failing to obtain even a single morsel of food and being beaten with wood, stones, gravel, and the like, he approaches his mother while weeping for the broken bowl, becoming exceedingly full of grief.
He began to cry out.
Then, seeing him, she was distressed; striking her breast, she said:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Whose fault is this, my son? What could have happened to you?"
"By whom, casting aside compassion, has such a blow been struck at you while you were suffering?
Then the deformed youth, weeping aloud, said:
"To whichever house door I go to beg..."
“They are beating me with bricks, stones, wood, and so forth.
[2] Having heard this, the caravan leader’s wife embraced the deformed youth around the neck and, weeping aloud, said:
"Surely you must have committed a terrible sin in previous births as a son, by which, despite being utterly defenseless, you are thus beaten by others. Alas!
What a tragedy!"
Upon seeing him so utterly devoid of flavor, destitute of happiness, wretched, and begging, compassion arose in her heart:
"Alas! I am ruined, I am destroyed! By whom, my son, has your bowl been taken?"

O son, by whom has your alms-bowl been broken today— broken by one whose own body is broken, who subsists on mere alms, who is abandoned by father and mother, and who is himself liberated from the householder’s life? (3-4)
For you whose entire lineage has perished and who are shunned by your kinsmen, who is your friend, your protector, and your teacher? By whom was your bowl broken?
Alas, my son! By whom was such violence shown toward you while you were so afflicted?
"Alas! You are destroyed, my poor son; you have been slain by your own past karma.
Alas, my son! Who is so gentle yet so brave? Tell me now, whose heart does compassion not penetrate? Whose heart is as hard as a stone or a rock?"

Alas! How can the minds of people bring themselves to strike you down—you who are wretched, ruined by hundreds of misfortunes, wandering for alms, afflicted by suffering, exhausted by hunger and thirst, and utterly destitute of all prosperity? (8)
Alas! Who would strive to kill one who is tormented by the suffering of disease and already ruined?
Having seen him today—miserable, with a dejected face, weeping, oppressed by hunger, and with a parched throat—why has no compassion been shown toward you?
"My son, how were you beaten by those agitated by the intoxication of pride in their caste?
Who has today abandoned compassion for you, who are overcome by pain and so deeply afflicted?
Alas! That which was earned by you through begging while tormented by hunger—"
That little food has even now been devoured by dogs and crows.
Alas, my son! I am ill-fated; what can I do for you now?
By the Creator, through previously committed sin, this undesirable deed has been wrought.

[90] Thus, lamenting for her son in many ways, she embraced him— his body drenched in streams of blood— as he lay before that very ruined hut on ground filled with a great deal of refuse, gravel, filth, stumps, and thorns.
Having sat down on the ground, she began to caress him gently with her hand.

Then she saw many sons of guild-masters and caravan leaders, as well as other prominent brahmins and householders, passing along the middle of the street, their bodies adorned with various magnificent and colorful garments— Kāśika, dukūla, koṭambaka, and kauśeya silks, as well as fine and most precious fabrics— and decorated with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, bangles, earrings, strings of pearls, and half-necklaces.

Beholding those whose bodies were adorned with clusters of various blooming fragrant flowers, and seeing his own exceedingly wretched condition as well as that son of his who was so deformed and possessed such a most piteous countenance, she heaved a long and hot sigh and spoke aloud in words full of tears and extreme despondency:
Having been born into a vast lineage filled with a hundred perfect qualities and resembling the ocean in its jewels, and having experienced supreme happiness,
they have now become sharers in misfortune, dwelling within the belly of a refuse heap.

Even with great difficulty, we two, hungry as we were, could not obtain food. Alas, alas! Crying out "We are ruined!", we have entered this ocean of poverty—a sea whose terrifying waves are a web of sorrows, strewn with hundreds of fierce crocodiles that are anguish, and filled with a flood of water that is destitution. //2-3//

They have indeed entered the river of poverty, which is crowded with thousands of crocodiles of misfortune, turbulent with the waves and surges of terrifying calamities, and fierce with the fear of being pierced by great diseases; it is strewn with the harsh stones of suffering and sickness, and its thickets are filled with the lion’s roar of anguish. 4.
We have entered this abode of poverty and suffering, strewn with hundreds of nests for the birds of grief.
Surely in the past, no gift was given by us to virtuous people, for our intentions were faltering due to negligence;
thus we now behold these ever-proud faces, wretched and ill-fated as we are. (5-6)
"Most likely, because we were deluded by our own impotence and lack of fortune, we did not give alms to the beggar who came to us;
for which reason we have been born as eunuchs, deprived even of a dwelling, and have fallen into this most terrible calamity.
Surely, having encountered those who are esteemed as gurus on this earth, we insulted them after having honored them."
By which we have now become objects of contempt and are today sharing in the misfortune of the people;
(8) surely many [beings] were struck while in restraint during previous births, since this person strikes us with stones and clods of earth. (9)
Surely our elders were led onto the path of reproach in a former life,
since such a painful and most dreadful humiliation has now befallen us;
for we did not give [anything] to guests in our previous birth.
By whom our garments have now become no more than rags;
12/ by whom many people were made to raise a great clamor of weeping, so that we, deprived of our kinsmen, may weep for a long time in sorrow. 13/
In the past, you did not give a bed covered with a variegated cloth, because of which you now sleep upon the bare ground strewn with gravel and stones;
nor did you offer various beautiful seats to the virtuous. (14)
The earth is our seat, though it is crowded with many thorns;
for we have never before given shoes, nor have we provided any comfortable vehicle by which we might travel upon the ground strewn with thorns. (15–16)
Indeed, out of stinginess regarding our dwelling, we generally gave nothing at all to those who came as supplicants, not even the mere shelter of our home;
it is for that reason that we have arrived here at this heap of refuse, its center illuminated by the rows of fierce rays [of the sun].
Having previously observed those whose throats were parched, whose cheeks and faces were withered, and whose minds longed for a drink—
"Surely no cool water was given by them, for which we are now so excessively parched in the mouth.

(18) No food was ever given by us to a wretched person, nor were kinsmen, nor friends, nor circles of relatives honored and fed with food according to the proper rites; therefore, deprived of sustenance here, we wander about. (19)
Surely we must have been provoked in many ways by those who, in other lives, were skilled in practicing for the benefit of others;

for because of that, even now, we have come to be the objects of abuse for others in this world as well. (20) Surely, on account of our reliance on the intoxication of pride in our birth, many [beings]—by us two—[have been harmed].
By whom, though they were virtuous, have they now been made harsh through being beaten?
(21) By whom was that medicine not given in the past—which removes all diseases and fears—to the mind in the ocean of *saṃsāra*, so that it is now tormented by illnesses? (22)
Neither their paternal friends nor their mother, neither their father nor their teachers, nor the wretched folk were ever bathed by him;

for he was born here according to destiny, struck down by a fortune of a hundred sorrows, helpless, deprived of bathing and drink, exhausted by hunger and thirst, and destitute of food and clothing. (23)
Afflicted by the suffering of disease, who indeed will protect us?
To whom shall we be slaves today, or whose attendants shall we be? Who might grant us life today, which is so very difficult to obtain in this world? (24–25)
"Alas, poverty is indeed suffering! Alas, too, is the lack of merit!
For even though this city is so prosperous, there is no protector for us two," she said.
Thus, in various ways, the caravan leader's wife remained there, her heart overwhelmed by hunger, lamenting for herself.
[91] And the caravan leader Karṇa, having had his ship wrecked in the great ocean, somehow reached a plank and, accompanied by a boy, emerged from the water onto dry land.
Wandering for alms with great hardship, he arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
He arrived there for the night's lodging in a field outside the village.
There, a certain hired laborer acting as a field-guard recognized him.
This thought occurred to the guard: "This caravan leader has arrived accompanied by his son; his body is exceedingly emaciated, and his entire store of wealth and property has been lost."

Thinking, "How shall I announce his entry into the household? Rather, he will know it himself," Karṇa the caravan leader gave him water for washing his hands and presented two bean cakes. Then, Karṇa the caravan leader set aside one bean cake, thinking, "I must not enter the house empty-handed," and placed it in the hand of the boy.
Thus, having divided it into half-portions, he was devoured along with that boy by that body which required no food.
Then, on another day, the caravan leader Karṇa, taking that bean-cake, entered the capital city of Bandhumatī with a body exceedingly parched and emaciated, his sole possession being a single,
extremely dirty garment, and set out for his home.
[92] Even Virūpa, at the very time of dawn, his face emaciated by hunger and thirst, said to his mother: "What purpose is there for me, unfortunate as I am, in remaining here or even in living?
I shall go; I will put an end to myself."

"Mother, I am going to my father's garden," he said, and set out for that garden. Karṇa, the caravan leader, having gone near his own home, saw after a long time his son, whose complexion was like the color of a peaceful dwelling.
Seeing that only a heap of earth remained, he thought again, "What is this? and entered that ruined cell.
As soon as he looked, he saw his wife staying in that ruined cell together with a maidservant;
she was exceedingly emaciated, her face was wretched, her waist was covered by a tattered, soiled rag, and her limbs were scorched by a layer of grime. Upon seeing her, [he...]

And again, having exclaimed, "Alas! What is this?", he fell to the ground in a swoon. Upon being touched by a cool breeze, he regained consciousness after a long time and, together with his wife, began to cry out loudly, "What is this? Then, having learned the news from his wife, he sighed deeply and hotly and said:
"Surely I have not performed acts of service toward the field of those worthy of offerings, which is why such a calamity has befallen me.
What shall I do now? To whom shall I go for refuge?
Whose face shall I look upon?"
Who in the world is compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched?

Having approached whom shall I cross this great ocean of poverty? Having approached whom shall I wash away the mire of misfortune? Having approached whom shall I cross this endless river of sorrow? Having approached whom shall I defeat this enemy of poverty? Having approached whom shall I uproot this creeper of poverty, which is the matrix of all suffering? Having approached whom shall I pull out this tree of poverty?
Resorting to whom shall I expel this great rākṣasa of poverty, whose mouth is made terrifying by the fangs of the pain of hunger and who utters the dreadful, great roar of "Alas, alas"?
Resorting to whom shall I defeat this great wrestler of poverty?
Resorting to whom shall I extinguish this fire that increases poverty, whose blazing flames are hunger, thirst, and the like?

Whom shall I rely upon to subdue this great elephant of poverty, smeared with the ichor of despair? Whom shall I rely upon to render poisonless this great serpent of poverty, whose venomous breath consists of manifold sufferings? Whom shall I rely upon to ward off this great thief of poverty, who carries away everything?
Having relied upon whom shall I shatter this chain of poverty, which is by its very nature all suffering? Having relied upon whom shall I pass beyond this prison of poverty?
Having relied upon whom shall I split open this door-panel of poverty?
"Whom shall I approach so that I may dispel this destroyer of poverty?
Whom shall I approach so that I may cross over this flood of despair?
Whom shall I approach so that I may traverse this great wilderness of poverty? Thus he cried out with many kinds of piteous, wretched, and faltering words.
In this interval, there is nothing whatsoever unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Blessed Buddhas;
for such is the very nature (dharmatā) of the Blessed Buddhas.

[For those] whose cages of birth, old age, and death have been shattered by the mass of rays from auspicious beams—[beams] which are like a cluster of young sunbeams inlaid with a multitude of autumnal dawn-rays, like a mass of stainless young sprouts of precious gems, like blue lotuses, emeralds, and the gentle-rayed moon, like a circle of pure lightning, and like a profusion of flames from a sacrificial fire well-nourished by streams of ghee.

[The faces] of those whose eyebrows are thick with the jewel-like radiance of a fathom-wide halo—soft, glossy, clockwise-turning, and white as the moon with its hundred eyes in the infinite sky; shining with stainless rays emitted from hands curved like the beautiful bow of Indra, which rests upon the tips of hundreds of millions of *jāmbūnada* gold vessels fashioned by the concentrated power of many hundreds of virtues; resembling the *kumuda* lily, the conch, the *kuṭaja* flower, the jasmine vine, the pearl necklace, frost, the lotus stalk, the pure tusk of an elephant, and the curved peak of Mount Meru;
and whose faces shine like blossomed fresh lotuses, having been perfected through three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

[To those] who have increased the equipment for unsurpassed enlightenment through the renunciation of hands, feet, eyes, faces, heads, their own flesh and blood, wives and children as lovely as young lotuses, elephants, horses, chariots, ornaments, garments, food, seats, beds, jewels, gold, silver, all their possessions, and even their kingdoms;
who are free from attachment; and who, by crushing the power of the bodiless one (Māra), are garlanded with thousands of masses of radiant fame as pure as the orb of the autumn moon.

Their forms were enveloped by a halo of pure radiance, like a mass of campaka flowers drawn forth from a vaidūrya stone— the belly of the lord of serpents, resembling the petals of a lotus, the crescent moon, the orb of the moon, the jewel of the makara, the harsh crest of the flame of the fire, the bow of the moon, the dense sprouts shimmering upon the ocean of the netherworld (pātāla) agitated by the golden mountain’s *rucaka* peak pierced by the spear-like tusks of Indra’s elephant, and the thousand streaks of lightning emerging from the clouds of the gathered rays of the young sun, whose orb was matted with the creeper-like rays of the moon as it rose over the king of the eastern mountains.

To those whose dense thickets of mental afflictions have been reduced to ashes by the fire of knowledge realized within themselves; whose lotus-feet are colored by the sprinkling of golden and jeweled crests from the crowns of thousands of gods prostrating before them;
whose copper-hued feet possess the brilliance of a cluster of *śoka* flowers, a mass of twilight clouds, a lake of lotuses, and the thick red lac from the palate of a young elephant;
and whose stainless lotus-feet bear the smile of the moonlight of their slender, copper-colored nails.
To those who have uprooted the creepers of craving, who have destroyed the entire darkness of delusion,
who have become kinsmen to the whole world, and whose nature is that of supreme, disinterested affection;
To those whose sphere of activity is inconceivable wisdom;
who have grasped the great horn of the serpent of passion; who have accumulated the equipment of the multitude of supreme qualities acquired through hundreds of thousands of difficult feats;
and who have uprooted the entire trunk of the tree of afflictions by the power of wisdom earned through the accumulation of merit.

To those whose commands are praised by the gods—Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Anala, Anila, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śāna, and Āpa; who are possessed of great compassion; and who are engaged in bestowing grace upon the world.
They were guardians of the single [practice], peerless,
proponents of non-duality,
dwellers in calm abiding and insight, and skilled in the three bases of self-mastery.
To those who have crossed over the four floods,
whose feet are well-established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power,
who have long practiced familiarity with the four means of attraction, who are free from the five factors, and who have transcended the five destinies.
To those endowed with the six limbs,

[101] Although the boy Virūpa had entered his father’s garden, his mind was tormented by the suffering of hunger; repeatedly lamenting his own extreme deformity, he reflected:
"What purpose is there in living for me, a doer of evil deeds, a partaker of supreme misery, so exceedingly deformed and unfortunate to behold?
I shall certainly destroy myself. With a distressed mind, he suddenly [seized] the highest branch of a *pāṭala* tree.
He climbed onto a tree branch, which suddenly broke; falling together with the branch, he remained there, afflicted by pain.
In this interval, there is nothing whatsoever unknown or unseen by the Blessed Buddhas.

The Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin, with his purified divine Buddha-eye which transcends the human, saw Virūpa, unknown and disregarded, suffering in such a manner; and having seen him, being impelled by his great compassionate duty, he went to that place by means of supernatural power and emitted the radiance of his own body.
And the rays of the Blessed One’s loving-kindness, accumulated over hundreds of eons, were released.

As soon as he was touched by them, the painful sensations in Virūpa’s body vanished, and that suffering of hunger and thirst was stilled. He rose up suddenly and beheld Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One—whose sight is difficult to obtain even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—with a body radiant with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; and upon seeing the Blessed One, his [suffering]...

Faith arose in him toward the perfectly enlightened Buddha Vipaśyin. He was wearing a piece of cloth, one cubit in length, dyed with turmeric; overcome by that faith, he took it off from his body and, with great impetus of devotion, immediately cast it over the Teacher Vipaśyin.
And there was a single *karṇikāra* flower, which had been empowered by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha Vipaśyin,
such that it became the size of the Tathāgata’s body and covered his body;
and the *karṇikāra* flower, having become as large as a seated cartwheel, remained positioned like a parasol.
Upon seeing that, an immense faith arose in the boy Virūpa.
With a great surge of devotion, he prostrated at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin and began to make a vow in a loud voice:
"O Best of Bipeds, by this gift, may my ugliness here [be removed]..."
From this day forward, having completely cast [my old form] aside, may I obtain a beautiful appearance; may I be clothed in garments of golden hue, enveloped in a brilliance like that of gold,
and may the fragrance of sandalwood and blue lotuses issue from my body and my mouth.

Resembling the color of gold, he is enchanting to all the world; he is liberated from all diseases and has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures. He is endowed with all forms of speech and is devoid of all that is meaningless.

May I become the most excellent of all, the seer of all, adorned with every form; may I be a perfectly awakened Buddha who accomplishes the welfare of all, compassionate toward sentient beings, endowed with all stainless qualities, glorious, possessed of all requisites, and happy. 4–5.

and the deities let fall a great rain of flowers, including *karṇikāra*, blue lotus, *campaka*, red lotus, white lotus, and *māndāraka*.

A rain of divine sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, and *tamāla* leaf powder was released, and thus it was proclaimed: "Oh! From the seed of generosity sown toward the Tathāgata, a most desirable and distinguished sprout has arisen!

Then the caravan leader, traveling with rapid strides, arrived at that park and beheld the youth Virūpa,

"Child, whose son are you?
He replied, "I am the son of the caravan leader named Karṇa.

He said, "Alas! I have been thoroughly mocked by this prince.

The youth Virūpa, his eyes wide with joy, spoke in a loud voice:
