And where is this great crystal [floor], into the edges of which sapphire has entered? 13–14.
Where is that former seat, devoid of furniture and consisting of nothing more than a single brick; and where is this [present one], adorned with variegated cloths, fine sheets, and cushions?
Where is that former bed upon the ground strewn with gravel? 15.
Where is this broad silk canopy, so delightful and majestic?
16/ Where is that bed of mine, so exceedingly harsh, spread upon the bare ground?
And where is this [bed] now spread with cotton wool, so exceedingly delightful? 17/
Where is that house, its interior filled with dogs and reeking with foul odors;
and where is this palace, its inner apartments perfumed with fragrant scents?
Where is that former dwelling, both inside and out covered in rags and tattered cloth? (18)
Where is this [body], charming with its variegated ornamentation of various excellent jewels?
(19) Where is that [body] draped with hundreds of impure white lines like crows? And where is this [body] adorned with many large pearl necklaces? (20)
Where is that house with its arms raised high in lamentation for suffering, and where is this place adorned by the uplifted shadow of stainless parasols and banners?
Homage be to that Protector, the field of merit, the Savior! 21.
Having relied upon whom I have this very day crossed the ocean of poverty—
homage be to the Lord of the World, the Omniscient Vipaśyin!
Having relied upon whom such prosperity as this has been attained by me this very day.

Having approached that Teacher, who is like the inconceivable Vaijayanta palace, adorned with manifold virtues, and by whom I have this very day attained this supreme abode; he who rises high as the peak of Kailāsa— 24.
Having reached this lofty mansion, white as the autumn moon, he has this very day become the master of this city;
having been afflicted by the suffering of poverty, he has this very day attained the preeminence of those possessing great wealth. (25–26)
"That seed which, sown this very day, yields fruit for me—
what person would not worship that All-pervading Lord, the Best in the World?

[109] Then Karṇa, the caravan leader, his mental continuum overwhelmed by the force of intense faith, reflected: "It is by relying on the Blessed One that I have obtained such prosperity; what if I were to first invite the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, along with his community of disciples, into this house and provide them with a meal? Having understood this, he prepared a great reception.
Having invited the Tathāgata Vipaśyin together with his community of disciples to his home, he fed them for seven days with food of a hundred flavors;
then, prostrating at their feet, he offered them all necessary requisites for as long as he lived.

[110] Then, on another day, at dawn, that field-guarding laborer took the food packet provided by his master and set out for the field; on the way, that laborer heard from a certain lay follower (upāsaka) how the caravan leader Karṇa, having offered a single bean-cake to the Blessed Buddha, had attained such a state.
Having heard that "the Blessed One has arrived," that man spoke again to the lay follower:
"O virtuous one, what are the qualities of that Blessed One?
That lay follower replied:
"O gentle-faced one, what power do I have to describe the specific qualities of that Blessed One?
Listen, however, to a single summary:
for that Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, is adorned with the marks of a supreme person, shines like a mountain of gold, and possesses a radiance exceeding that of the moon and the sun."

Gentle, firm in his vows, peaceful in mind, eloquent in speech, well-adorned, with beautiful limbs, a beautiful face, and beautiful eyes; one of good deeds and true dharma, patient, possessed of presence of mind;
a leader, a good guide, knowing the right course, knowing self-restraint, grateful, keen-sighted, with senses perfectly tranquil, and whose horses of the senses are well-trained.

The great King of Dharma, the essence of great beings, the great protector of the world, the banner of great wisdom, the hero among great speakers, the treasury of great merit, the cause of the great Dharma, the great caravan leader, the giver of Dharma, the great helmsman, the one most worthy of offerings; the cutter of thirst, the destroyer of great delusion, the extinguisher of anger, the establisher in liberation, the one who turns away from evil paths, and the pointer to the true path.

He is the cutter of doubt, the revealer of truth, the extinguisher of afflictions, the destroyer of Māra, the savior of the world, worshipped by Brahmā, honored by Śakra, superior to all worlds, the benefactor of all worlds, the supreme among beings, the ender of all suffering, and the omniscient one.
He is skilled in both worldly conduct and discipline, has transcended all outflows (*āsrava*), is not surpassed by the foremost of disputants, and is unconfounded by any faults.

Exerting himself for the sake of all, he is handsome, virtuous, meditative, energetic, and endowed with wisdom; likewise, he is free from longing, free from feverish distress, free from conceptual proliferation, and his livelihood is effortless. He demonstrates the means for the cessation of worldly activity, possesses a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, is liberated from evil, and is endowed with resolute conviction. He is the unsurpassed leader and guide, acting as a great physician for those afflicted by the disease of the mental afflictions.

The Self-Existent One, the all-pervading Lord, whose self is restrained, whose power is immeasurable, who has accomplished little yet is perfectly contented, who possesses mastery over time, who is endowed with purpose and wisdom, who has conquered the enemy of the afflictions, whose fires are extinguished, whose nature is unshakeable, and who is a supreme object of veneration— having beheld the world in extreme suffering, submerged in the mire of ignorance, and being himself capable of lifting it out by means of his own power corresponding to his own nature; [he acts].
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, such is this most excellent resolve; therefore, I shall thus deliver the suffering world and liberate it.

How may I comfort those who are terrified? How may I uplift those submerged in saṃsāra? How may I gladden those who are burning? Having thus generated a firm mind and exerted supreme vigor throughout thousands of millions of births—

And as before, having cut off delightful food, drink, shelter, sandals, meals, umbrellas, vehicles, seats, and so forth— along with elephants, horses, wives, children, male and female slaves, his own eyes, and even his own flesh, together with phlegm and teeth— he, whose nature is the Buddha, being like a hawk, thought of the welfare of all sentient beings through every means at all times, [beholding them] as aged, sick, exhausted, bewildered, and agitated, by means of that thunderbolt-like wisdom.

Having observed all beings established [in suffering] and having comforted them— whether they were virtuous or non-virtuous— he, by serving his teachers and through qualities such as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, fortitude, wisdom, meditative concentration, and so forth, attained the supreme, auspicious awakening after many thousands of millions of births.
Furthermore, who is he, that most excellent of all beings, the Perfectly Awakened One of renowned fame, whose Dharma is characterized by compassion and inspires universal trust?

He had approached the presence of the Lord of the Universe— who was full of wisdom, possessed of vast vigor, one who had fulfilled all his vows, liberated from faults, extinguished in delusion, peaceful, self-controlled, and powerless toward the objects of all the senses; whose treasury of knowledge was adorned with the radiance of immeasurable power,
whose face surpassed the light of the full moon, and who is eternally worshipped with devotion and grace by the lords of the gods, the lords of the asuras, and the serpents.

Who is able to describe in their entirety the qualities of that Perfectly Awakened One— the Lord of Dharma, who possesses blazing splendor, whose fame is merit, who was born of a great seer, who has the radiance of molten gold, who has reached the further shore of the foremost dharmas, the supreme being, the Protector, the Naga, the Liberated One, the Steadfast, the Hero, the God beyond gods?
Moreover,
he was adorned with the perfection of all excellent forms and beauty.
No other being possesses such a supreme body as that of the Buddha.
There is no speaker equal to the Buddha; there is no wise one equal to the Buddha.
There is no awakened one equal to the Buddha; there is no wise one equal to the Buddha. (1–2)
There is no vessel equal to the Buddha; there is no one as happy as the Buddha.
There is no one as self-controlled as the Buddha; there is no one as sovereign as the Buddha.
There is no teacher equal to the Buddha; there is no father equal to the Buddha. (3)
There is no kinsman equal to the Buddha; there is no friend equal to the Buddha.
He is free from possessiveness, free from intoxication, fearless, free from weariness, and free from passion.
He has crossed the wilderness of existence; he is without rival and free from affliction. //4-5//
Charming, peaceful, pure, self-controlled, mindful, powerful, and masterful—there is no one equal to the Buddha for all sentient beings whose hearts he has won.
In brief, because he is endowed with excellent qualities and distinctions in accordance with the rule. (6)

"Let it be understood that even in the three worlds there is no one equal to the Buddha. (7) Having heard this, the hired man, his throat bristling with faith, suddenly possessed an exceedingly rare eloquence and said to him:
When the caravan leader Karṇa offered a bean-cake out of craving to the Blessed One Vipaśyin, the Tathāgata— who is such a supremely worthy recipient of offerings—

at that very moment, having encountered the Tathāgata who is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, he made a vow based on the mere cause of his extremely limited wealth, thinking: "May I become free from poverty."

But I, moreover, having failed to obtain a vision of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One— even after many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons— behold him who is most beautiful to behold, the unsurpassed one, whose compassion proceeds from the entire mass of supreme merit accumulated by all beings over hundreds of thousands of countless eons, who is compassionate toward those exceedingly wretched, bitten by the venomous serpents of the manifold afflictions of saṃsāra, and who is especially affectionate toward fallen people.
"I, who have been without assistance from kinsmen and have not acquired wealth for many ages, now approach you to provide this meager portion of cooked alms-food earned as a field-guardian.
Immediately upon the conclusion of these words uttered with such an intention— that I shall make such a vow by which I will become the supreme among all beings— "

The Blessed One, Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One, knowing the thought in his mind, went by means of his supernormal power and stood before him. That hired laborer beheld the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, whose appearance was most captivating; seeing his body’s radiance, which was exceedingly brilliant and illuminated from within by the spreading mass of the first rays of the morning sun upon the peak of the lovely, beautiful, and golden mountain of the gods, he was filled with supreme joy and gladness, and through the force of an immense surge of serene faith, [he offered] that bowl of food.
Having taken it and placed it in the alms-bowl of the Blessed One Vipaśyin, the perfectly enlightened one, he fell at his feet with a surge of intense faith and began to make a formal aspiration.
O Protector, by this merit, from this birth onwards,
may I be ever more devoted to the welfare of all sentient beings and possess a compassionate nature. (1)
Just as you, endowed with the marks, have attained unsurpassed awakening, so may I too fully attain the incomparable perfect awakening;
just as you teach the Dharma and just as you have attained omniscience. (2)
Just as you have attained it, may I likewise attain omniscience.
Just as Māra was conquered by you and the Wheel of Dharma was set in motion, so too, having conquered him, shall I set the Wheel of Dharma in motion. 3–4.
"O Protector, just as you have crossed over and now deliver many beings from the ocean of saṃsāra, so too, O Best of Sages, shall I cross over.
Then the Blessed One, Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One, spoke aloud with a voice as deep and majestic as a full rain-cloud:
"O gentle-faced one! Then that Blessed One, Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One, spoke aloud with a voice as deep and sublime as the entire mass of clouds:
'O gentle-faced one!'"
"For you, O one of great majesty, shall indeed become a teacher on earth named Sarvārthasiddha;
having forcibly conquered here Māra together with his army, who was terrifyingly surging forth from all sides.

[114] Then, having prophesied that man’s attainment of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin departed; and this news spread throughout the royal capital of Bandhumatī,
until it was heard by King Bandhumat.

Having heard this, he himself came there with a mind encouraged by the accumulation of those roots of merit; he placed that man upon the back of an elephant with great honor, led him to his palace, seated him on half of his own throne, and honored him by bestowing half of his kingdom.
He then said:
"Great King, I have no need for sensual pleasures; therefore, grant me permission so that I may go forth and practice the holy life.

Having been granted permission by the king, he went forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. There, having practiced the holy life to its full extent, he passed away and was reborn among the Nirmāṇarati gods.
King Bandhumat also passed away.
His son was established in the kingdom.

He too, having ruled the kingdom for some time, passed away; and by the ministers, with great honor, Surūpa was established in the kingdom. By him, the kingdom was ruled according to the Dharma for sixty thousand years.
Then, having passed away, he was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.
What do you think, Great King, was that King Surūpa at that time and on that occasion someone other than him?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;
rather, at that time and on that occasion, this Suvarṇavarṇa was the king named Surūpa,
by whom a piece of turmeric-dyed cloth was offered to the Tathāgata Vipaśyin and a formal vow was made.
As the ripening of that karma, he experienced infinite divine and human happiness among gods and men;
wherever he was reborn, there he possessed a golden body with a form clothed in golden-colored garments, and at the time of his birth, a rain of *karṇikāra* flowers would fall upon him.
Even now he is thus possessed of such great majesty of merit that whenever a garment is repeatedly removed from his body, another garment appears upon his person at that very moment.

He who was the caravan leader Karṇa at that time and on that occasion is this very same Divākara, the caravan leader; and she who was the wife of the caravan leader Karṇa is this very same wife of the caravan leader Divākara.
At that time and on that occasion, Kāśisundarī was the maidservant and Pracaṇḍa was the chief minister.
Furthermore, King Ajātaśatru spoke thus to the Elder Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, what karma was performed by the monk Suvarṇavarṇa,
the ripening of which resulted in his being impaled on a stake despite having done no harm and committed no offense,
yet after going forth he attained arhatship?"
The Elder Ānanda said:

"In the past, O Great King, in a time long gone, there appeared in the world a Perfectly Awakened One named Candra— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed."
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling having departed from a certain royal capital.

At that time, in a certain monastery, there was a certain monk who was a preacher of the Dharma; he taught the Dharma from time to time to the brahmins and householders who came to him, and great gain and honor accrued to him.
[Sva Roy 320,3 – 323,4] [117] Then, at another time, a monk named Ajita— a preacher of the Dharma, possessed of ready and liberated eloquence, a speaker of varied and sweet discourse—
while wandering on a tour of the countryside, arrived at that monastery. He taught the Dharma to the fourfold assembly, beginning with...
He proclaimed the holy life— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with excellent phrasing, entirely complete, pure,
and utterly radiant. By this, the entire population dwelling in that mountain village was inspired with deep faith.

He was a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. When his gains and honors were cut off by that resident monk who was a preacher of the Dharma, this thought occurred to him: "The monk Ajita has brought about the cessation of my gains and honors.
As long as he remains here, how will I obtain any gain or honor?"
"I must devise a means for him to go," he thought;
then he reflected further:
"Those who are deeply learned are indeed fearful of being treated with disrespect."
Thinking, "I must employ a disrespectful treatment toward him," he spoke to a certain Brahmin girl:
"Sister, I shall give you a pair of garments; corrupt this monk Ajita by saying, 'He has practiced unchastity with me.
She replied, "Noble sir, if I were to speak thus, who would ever marry me?"
"Surely I shall support my mother and father for as long as I live.
He replied, "I will act in such a way that it will not become known to the public,
once you speak with me in private conversation."
Moreover, when he remained here seated together with three or four other monks, she promised,
"I shall do so."
[118] Then, on another day, while that preacher of the Dharma was sitting at the door of his cell together with the monks, engaged in conversation, that brahmin girl went there and said to him:
"Noble sir, because you have gone forth as renunciants, we consider it appropriate to approach you here with confidence."
"How is this appropriate—that I have been forcibly seized by this monk Ajita and rendered a non-virgin?
Then those monks, covering their ears, said:
"Sister, do not speak thus; this is not to be heard."
Then that monk who was a preacher of the Dharma, saying "This was not well done! This was not well done!", uttered dispraise of the monk Ajita.
When this reached the monk Ajita through the succession of hearing, he heard it and said:
"Who says such a thing?"
"This is a monk who is a preacher of the Dharma.
He approached the monk who was a preacher of the Dharma;
having approached him, he said:
"Venerable sir, what offense have I committed against you that you have uttered such slander concerning me?
Having thus provoked a state of malice toward him, he uttered this harsh verbal action: "Such an evil deed has been committed by you that you deserve the stake.
Upon hearing this, it occurred to the monk Ajita:

Perceiving that this ascetic was suffering and afflicted, he took his bowl and robe, put away his bedding and seat exactly as he had used them, and having departed from that monastery, set out on his way.
Seeing him depart, the monks, the nuns, and the body of people living in that mountain village, desiring to turn him back, followed after him.

[119] Remorse arose in that monk who was a preacher of the Dharma: "It was not well done by me that, for the sake of gain and honor, I committed such an action leading to rebirth in the states of woe. Thus, dejection arose within him.

"I shall go and ask his forgiveness. Thinking thus, he departed very quickly from that monastery with a deeply agitated mind, his wretched face drenched by streams of tears, weeping loudly like a young child.
While those many hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders looked on, he fell at the feet of the monk Ajita and began to confess his transgression as a transgression.

"Forgive me, Venerable One! Just as I was childish, deluded, unrefined, and unskilled, and overcome by gain and honor, I uttered a false disparagement of you; therefore, confess this transgression from its very root, forgive me, and have compassion for me.
Thus spoke the monk Ajita.
The Venerable One, having said, "It is well," sat down at the foot of a certain tree with a deeply agitated mind;
having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, he—
by means of that very mind made fluid by supreme spiritual urgency— exerted himself, strove, and labored toward this very [goal].
Having understood the five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and shifting, he became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra; then,
like a king of swans with outspread wings, he soared into the expanse of the sky and began to display various miracles, gladdening the minds of that great multitude of people.

And that monk, the preacher of the Dharma, having looked up at him in the expanse of the sky, cried out, "Alas, what a tragedy! I have harbored a malicious thought toward such a great seer," and having said this, he fell to the ground in a swoon.
In the meantime, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, his heart permeated with great compassion,
perceived that this monk who was preaching the Dharma might indeed die after vomiting hot blood.
Having arrived at that Karvaṭaka by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*),

the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, touched the head of that monk who was a preacher of the Dharma with his hand— a hand marked with wheels, svastikas, and *nandyāvarta* symbols, joined by a web, produced from hundreds of various merits, and capable of providing comfort to the frightened.
As soon as he was touched by the Blessed One, that monk regained his senses, rose up, and began to confess his transgression as a transgression.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, spoke these verses:
"For a person who is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which he cuts himself by speaking ill-spoken words. (1)
He who praises a person who deserves blame and blames a person who deserves praise gathers with his own mouth that misfortune among misfortunes by which he shall not find happiness.
(2) For this is indeed a minor misfortune, when one loses one's own wealth here through dice.
This is the greater evil here: that one should corrupt the mind toward the Sugatas.
For one hundred thousand *nirarbudas* and thirty-six plus five *arbudas*—these are the hells which the reviler of the Noble Ones enters, having directed his speech and mind toward evil. (3–4)
Because of the corruption of the mind, sentient beings go to an evil destination; because of the clarity of the mind, sentient beings go to a good destination. 5.
Thus the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, having gladdened that assembly with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
"What do you think, Great King? Was that monk who was a preacher of the Dharma at that time and on that occasion someone else?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way; rather, it was this very Suvarṇavarṇa who, at that time and on that occasion, was his..."
Having harbored malice toward a monk, he uttered harsh words; as the ripening of that karma, after falling into the hells for five hundred births,

he was born among humans and, for five hundred births, though innocent and harmless, was impaled on a stake— even now, by the power of that very same karma, though innocent and harmless, he has been impaled on a stake, provided that this karma [has not yet been exhausted].
If he had not confessed his transgression as a transgression, he would have been cooked for five hundred births in each of the great hells;
he would have been reborn among the hungry ghosts for five hundred births and among the animals for five hundred births.
However, because he practiced the holy life under the teaching of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, [the result of that]—
Through the ripening of that karma, he has now gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and, by abandoning all defilements, has realized arhatship.
Therefore, Great King, one who seeks to eliminate suffering for oneself must not harbor malice toward others.
"One who fears ill-repute should not attribute ill-repute to others;
one who seeks happiness for oneself must also bring about happiness for others. While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained a great distinction.
Some attained the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, and some the fruit of non-returning; some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions;
some generated the aspiration for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and some for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Some took up the training precepts for going for refuge;
for the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and gravitating toward the Saṅgha.
Then the caravan leader Divākara, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence and said this to the Elder Ānanda:
“Noble Ānanda, I have invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to my home and provided them with food of six flavors.”
"I thought that after feeding them, each individual monk should be clothed in a robe worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold];
yet that Blessed One has passed into parinirvāṇa. Therefore, I now wish to feed the community of monks, headed by the Venerable Ānanda."
The Elder Ānanda said, "Caravan leader, do as you say; I shall act in such a way that all the Blessed One’s disciples residing in Jambudvīpa will come here.
Then the caravan leader Divākara, his mind filled with great joy, went outside the city of Rājagṛha to the circular arena.
Having had it made exceedingly beautiful—cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel; with banners and flags raised high; sprinkled with sandalwood water; draped with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands;

strewn with various flowers; hung with incense burners and censers of fragrant smoke; and adorned with most lovely canopies and archways—and having prepared pure and exquisite solid foods that very night, he rose early in the morning and arranged the seats.
Having prepared the water-jars and established them, he informed the Elder Ānanda of the time by means of a messenger:
"Venerable sir, the time has come; the meal is ready; please do as you deem it timely now. (Sva Roy 339,3 – 341,5)

[123] Then the Elder Ānanda, having leaped into the expanse of the sky by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), illuminated this entire Jambudvīpa with a radiance having the luster of molten gold.
Striking the gong himself, he proclaimed in a voice as deep and clear as a water-bearing cloud:
"Those disciples of the Blessed One who have attained supernatural power, let them come by their own supernatural power; and those who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*..."
"Let them come by means of my supernatural power.
Then, having heard that gong, [beings] from the Himavat, Vindhya, Malaya, Pāriyātraka, Gandhamādana, Sumeru, Yugandhara, Īṣādhāra, Khadiraka, Sudarśana, Aśvakarṇa, Nimindhara, and other mountains;
from the forests, rivers, the Susītā, oceans, ports, excellent trees, monasteries, and dwellings; and from threshing floors, empty houses, cemeteries, and so forth—[all came].

And those monks who dwell having attained the bliss of meditative concentration, at that very moment, covering this entire expanse of the sky with masses of clouds as red as the *aśoka* and *kiṃśuka* flowers, as if with the crimson glow of twilight, came to the city of Rājagṛha and descended into that circular arena.
At that very moment, thirty million bhikṣuṇīs assembled:
one group of those whose outflows were exhausted,
and a second group of those still in training.
The third [assembly] consisted of ordinary virtuous persons; then, according to their seniority, they sat down each upon their own respective seats as they had been assigned.

[124] Then the caravan leader Divākara, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the noble Elder Ānanda was comfortably seated, personally satisfied them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.

When he perceived that the community of monks had finished eating, washed their hands, and set aside their bowls, and when he desired to clothe them with three robes each worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, he looked upon that community of monks and became joyful in mind.
Suvarṇavarṇa, understanding his intention, said: "Be free from anxiety."
"I myself shall clothe the community of monks with the three robes, golden-yellow in color."

Then, at that very moment, the monk Suvarṇavarṇa took off his gold-yellow garments one by one from his own body and bestowed the three robes upon the three crores of monks according to their seniority, each set being worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
In the meantime, thousands of deities uttered cries of "Alas! Alas!
and played various musical instruments;
they released a rain of divine flowers, while the multitude of people who had arrived from various regions and directions, as well as King Ajātaśatru, looked on.

Accompanied by his harem, princes, ministers, and the people of the city and countryside, he beheld that such marvel; with eyes wide open in wonder, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times: "Oh, the ripening of the fruit of merit! Oh, the power of meritorious deeds!
Oh, the ripening of the seed of generosity planted in a field worthy of offerings has not failed! What wise person, indeed, having observed such a ripening of the fruit of merit..."
"In that field worthy of offerings, no gift should be given"— thus did many hundreds of thousands of living beings, placing their joined palms upon their heads,
cry out loudly, "Homage to the Buddha! Then, the Elder Ānanda performed the dedication of the merit.

[125] Then the caravan leader Divākara rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Elder Ānanda, uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
"Venerable sir, this has not been done for us by mother, nor by father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives."
"By the former deceased Śravaṇa Brāhmaṇas, through their joy, that which was done for us has dried up the oceans of blood and tears."
O Sage, worshipped by the Daityas, humans, and gods in this world; free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
your vision, so difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes, has become fruitful today.
(Sva Roy 346,3–5)

[126] Then the Elder Ānanda, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that assembly including the king with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed while being paid homage by those hundreds of thousands of deities and many hundreds of thousands of living beings residing in Rājagṛha.
Thus, even a small act performed toward the Blessed Buddha yields no small fruit. [The verse begins: "Of those phenomena that arise from a cause... [Sva Roy 346,5–347,3] ...the cause... (6)
The Tathāgata has indeed taught of them, and of their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
(1) This is the religious gift of the Śākya bhikṣu Buddhākaragupta, a follower of the most excellent Mahāyāna; whatever merit is herein...
May this merit, having placed the teachers, preceptors, mother, and father at its head, lead to the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed knowledge for the entire mass of sentient beings.
